articles.title: Lindsay Clancy back in court seeking to dismiss murder charges after mistrial
articles.summary:
Lawyers for Massachusetts mother who killed children argue new trial would violate double jeopardy rules

Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Monday in an attempt to dismiss the charges that…

blocks.text: Lindsay Clancy returned to court on Monday in an attempt to dismiss the charges that she murdered her three young children.
The hearing Monday was the second time the Massachusetts mother has been in court since her trial ended with a deadlocked jury in September after jurors were unable to agree on a verdict.

Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behavior. Prosecutors have acknowledged that the 36-year-old Clancy had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong.
The focus of the hearing in front of Judge William Sullivan was a motion from the defense to dismiss the charges on double jeopardy grounds.

At Monday’s hearing, defense attorney Martin G Weinberg argued that Sullivan should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the lone holdout juror, Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations – potentially avoiding the mistrial, he said.
Kevin Reddington, another attorney representing Clancy, urged the court to examine Desronvil’s juror questionnaire, alleging that he had been dishonest in his responses.
Reddington also said he had evidence that Desronvil used his phone during deliberations and he allegedly researched altruistic filicide, USA Today reports.
Upon using Desronvil’s name, Sullivan said: “I’m going to stop you right there,” to which Reddington responded: “No, you’re not going to stop me.”
Sullivan went on to say that there was “no need here in this courtroom to use that” juror’s name, according to the Boston Globe.
In response, Reddington said: “He’s got more face time than I do,” appearing to refer to Desronvil’s media appearances following the trial.
Reddington also urged the court to determine whether Desronvil had conducted any research related to the trial, which could have warranted his dismissal.
Jennifer Sprague, a Plymouth county assistant district attorney, pushed back, saying: “If the door is open to examining this juror, it would be open on all jurors,” the New York Times reports.

After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminded them of their duties and explained what constitutes reasonable doubt. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes.

But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations.
“That’s what the foreperson was asking the court to do,” Weinberg said. “I can see that this is not easy,” he told the judge at one point.
“You don’t have to keep saying that – I have thick skin,” Sullivan replied.

Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague argued that Sullivan had struck the right balance in his handling of the jury. Pressing the foreperson further would have required delving into the substance of the jury’s deliberations, potentially inserting the court’s “interpretation of what is correct” into the process.
“You were the one who looked them in the eyes and asked them the questions and was in the best position to judge their credibility,” she told Sullivan. “And you credited their answers.”
Sprague argued that the holdout juror’s disagreement was not based on personal reasons, but on his belief that Clancy was guilty.
“It is clear from the record that this juror did not refuse to deliberate,” she said. “He refused to agree.”
Since the trial ended, Desronvil said he was certain of Clancy’s guilt but that no one would listen to him.

Desronvil released a statement after the trial, saying he “didn’t have any doubts” during the deliberation process, adding: “Based on all the physical evidence, key witnesses and what the prosecution presents, I thought it was enough proof that she (Clancy) knew exactly what she was doing and planned.”
Roni Carlson, the jury’s foreperson, told NBC10 in September that the single holdout juror “admitted he had reasonable doubt, and I started filling out the forms, I was so excited”.

“There were three forms I had to fill out and I started filling them out, I wrote my signature on each one, and then he said: ‘But I’m still not going to say that she’s not guilty by reason of insanity,’” she said.
Prosecutors argue that double jeopardy “does not bar the Commonwealth from seeking justice on behalf of the three victims.”

Additionally, Sprague requested a gag order prohibiting statements made outside the courtroom, citing what she characterized as Reddington’s “inappropriate” comments to the media, including his remark that he hoped the holdout juror could “sleep well at night”.
Reddington’s comments were “calculated to affect the public’s perception of the case”, according to Sprague. Sullivan said he would take the motion under advisement.
Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He also asked prosecutors how they intended to proceed with the case, prompting Sprague to respond: “We’re not at that point yet.”
He scheduled a hearing on 16 November to revisit the case and potentially set a retrial date.
Reddington argued against further delays, warning that they could result in a new judge taking over the case given Sullivan’s mandatory retirement in June next year.
“I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three,” Reddington said, adding: “I want a trial and I want it with you and I want it this spring.”
Sullivan said a trial in March is “probably realistic”.

articles.title: US to drop South Africa, Rwanda from duty-free trade initiative
articles.summary: The Trump administration has said South Africa and Rwanda are breaking the rules of the AGOA free trade initiative, a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.

image.caption: South Africa exported over $1.7 billion (€1.5 billion) in goods to the US under AGOA in 2025Image: Esa Alexander/REUTERS

blocks.text: South Africa and Rwanda are set to be removed from a US trade initiative that has provided duty-free access to the US market for thousands of products from sub-Saharan African countries for 26 years.

On Monday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said US President Donald Trump intends to "terminate" the two countries from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) trade preference program starting in January 2027.
The program, which comes under regular review, was extended in February by Trump.
In a statement, Greer said that "the governments of Rwanda and South Africa are engaging in practices that are inconsistent with AGOA's eligibility criteria."
Greer said these practices include "barriers that undermine American trade and investment and practices that pose a threat to US national security and foreign policy interests in the region."
The statement did not provide any specific examples of the trade barriers or security and foreign policy issues in question.
AGOA has expired — what's next for African trade and jobs?
What is AGOA?
AGOA was introduced in 2000 by former US President Bill Clinton, and it has become a centerpiece of US economic engagement with sub-Saharan Africa.
Duty free access to the US market is seen as a critical economic boost for the more than 30 AGOA countries. Over 1,800 specific products are covered under AGOA.

Requirements for membership include eliminating barriers to US trade and investment, while maintaining an open market economy along with democratic principles like the rule of law, human rights and labor protections.
South Africa largest AGOA partner
South Africa has been AGOA's largest beneficiary, with $1.7 billion (€1.5 billion) worth of goods like car parts, citrus fruit and wine, exported to the US under the program in 2025.

South Africa's Trade Ministry said last week that it was prepared for the decision, adding that AGOA exports comprise only about 10% of its ​total exports to the US and 1% of its total global exports.

blocks.caption: The government of South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has seen friction with the Trump administration [FILE: November 2023]Image: SIPHIWE SIBEKO/REUTERS

blocks.text: "AGOA remains important to South Africa, but it does not constitute the totality of the economic relationship between South Africa and the ‌United States," it said in a statement.
In recent weeks, President Cyril Ramaphosa has also said South Africa must prepare for being excluded from AGOA by seeking new markets and trade deals with partners like China.
On Monday, the South Africa government said the US remains an important trade partner and it would provide support for affected sectors.

South Africa's export-dependent citrus industry warned that its entire value chain "on both sides of the Atlantic, is now under threat," and warned that jobs and the economic security of entire communities is now at stake.
Rwanda sanctioned for alleged M23 ties
The US has been putting economic pressure on Rwanda over its alleged support of the M23 rebel group in the Democratic Republic of Congo.
Washington sanctioned Rwanda's Defense Ministry last week, which denies any ties to M23, along with several individuals, institutions and a gold refinery.
Major Rwandan exports to the US include coffee and minerals.

articles.title: ‘A despicable betrayal’: Democrats incensed by Haley Stevens’s endorsement of Mike Rogers
articles.summary:
Stevens’s decision sparked fierce backlash from members of the party, while Donald Trump praised the sudden switch

Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens’ shocking last-minute endorsement of Mike…

blocks.text: Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens’ shocking last-minute endorsement of Mike Rogers, a Republican Senate candidate, in the run-up to the elections has sparked fierce backlash from members of her party.

Stevens, who narrowly lost in the Democratic primary for Senate to Abdul El-Sayed, announced her support for Rogers after a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel.
Stevens had said she would appear at a campaign event if he denounced the advertisement. El-Sayed’s campaign disinvited her.

Following the extraordinary public rupture on Sunday, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised more than $2.4m, a fundraising record in the final days of a race that could determine control of the US senate. The Democrat’s campaign said more than 26,000 people contributed for the first time on Sunday.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, a Democrat from New York, described Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers as “a despicable betrayal”.

“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” Schumer posted on social media.
Nancy Pelosi, a California representative, posted that Stevens had “chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement”.
Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, also said that “working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday”.
“Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against,” Mamdani posted.

Stevens refused to clearly explain what led to her endorsement of Rogers in an interview with CNN on Sunday evening. “I’m just casting my one vote this way,” Stevens said, while insisting she still wanted Democrats to win the majority on election day.

“I am not trying to upset anyone,” she added. “I’m just being honest with my constituents and what I’m hearing from people, and in fact, I’ve been hearing from a ton of Dems, Anderson, who said: ‘Thank you, this is how we felt; we haven’t liked this campaign; it’s painful.’”

Cooper pressed Stevens on her decision, questioning whether being disinvited from El-Sayed’s campaign event triggered her endorsement of Rogers. At one point, Stevens refused to answer the question, allowing several seconds of silence to air.

Stevens has continued to defend her decision, as she faces accusations of betrayal from Democrats, including calls for her expulsion from the House caucus. Several members of her congressional staff resigned in protest. On Monday, she drew a parallel with Pennsylvania Senator John Fetterman, a one-time progressive who now frequently breaks with his party, especially over Israel.
“You see a Democrat from Pennsylvania, you know, his name’s a lightning rod in the party. His name’s Fetterman,” she told conservative commentator Scott Jennings. “They say the same thing about him.”
Curtis Hertel, the chair the Michigan Democratic party, said in a post that Stevens was not a member of the party “nor will she be in the future”.
A Detroit journalist, Sam Robinson, shared a video in which Hertel was asked why he thought Stevens made the endorsement.

“Obviously there are sour grapes from the election, but there is no reasonable explanation for this. I have known Haley Stevens for a long time, and I know what she has fought for her in her career, and this is the antithesis of all of that,” Hertel said.
Debbie Dingell, a Democratic representative from Michigan, said the state’s residents were focused on the cost of living, healthcare and housing.
“That’s what they’re talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens’ continued efforts to get attention,” she said in a statement.

On MS Now on Sunday, El-Sayed encouraged undecided Michigan voters to stand with him to protect democracy in the United States. “The divide in our politics isn’t left versus right; the divide in our politics is the people who are locked out versus the people who are locking them out,” El-Sayed said.

Speaking to Fox News on Monday, Rogers praised Stevens for her actions. “I know Democrats are thumping their chest and saying she has done something other than courageous,” he said. “It was nothing but courageous.”

While some Democrats and Jewish leaders also condemned the advertisement for El-Sayed, congressional nominees Brad Lander and Daniel Biss, both of whom are Jewish and Democrats, issued a statement on Sunday encouraging voters to support El-Sayed. They did not mention Stevens.

“In the closing days of this election, we must remember the true choice of this race,” the statement read. “One candidate represents a party that has stoked hatred, gutted anti-discrimination efforts and remained silent in the face of President Trump’s corruption and authoritarianism. The other represents the promise of accountability, affordability, and the fight for a more equitable, just, and democratic future.”

Meanwhile, Trump praised Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers on his platform Truth Social and described her as a “highly respected Democrat”. He continued to support Stevens during a campaign rally on Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, even going so far as to welcome her to join the Republican party.
“I’d love her to join the Republican party, actually, I think that could happen maybe. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan,” Trump said.
When asked about Trump praising her, Stevens told CNN: “Well, I impeached him twice,” before criticizing Republicans for being “really focused on just letting Trump be the dictator”.

articles.title: Ex-FBI chief in Chicago sues DoJ, claiming he was pressured to investigate Trump’s foes
articles.summary:
Douglas DePodesta says he was made ‘scapegoat’ after collapse of case against Broadview Six anti-ICE protesters

The former head of the FBI in Chicago has accused the Trump administration of…

blocks.text: The former head of the FBI in Chicago has accused the Trump administration of pressuring him to investigate the president’s political opponents and making him a “scapegoat” after a major federal case against anti-ICE protesters fell apart.

Douglas DePodesta, who served as FBI special agent in charge from 2024 until July 2026, alleged in a federal lawsuit filed on Monday that the Department of Justice (DoJ) had engaged in “misconduct” and “malfeasance” in its pursuit of unjust prosecutions – and that he was wrongly blamed for the DoJ’s missteps and unlawfully forced out of his job.
The suit names Kash Patel, the FBI director; Todd Blanche, the attorney general; and Andrew Boutros, the US attorney who leads the DoJ’s Chicago office.

DePodesta’s complaint alleges that Boutros pursued “politically motivated prosecutions” of protesters that turned into an “unprecedented disaster” for the DoJ and accuses the US attorney of making “intentionally” false statements to a judge.

DePodesta’s lawsuit provides a rare first-hand account from a senior FBI official of the fallout from the Trump administration’s aggressive efforts to criminally charge leftwing activists even when the charges are opposed by law enforcement officials.
During Operation Midway Blitz, ICE’s intense crackdown on Chicago last year, Boutros repeatedly pressured DePodesta to launch investigations that were “politically motivated”, the suit alleges.

On one occasion, Boutros was “openly hostile” when the FBI refused to write an affidavit saying a protester had “assaulted” an officer after the FBI reviewed video, which showed there was only “incidental touching as a result of the federal immigration agent’s tackling of the protester”, the complaint says.

“On other occasions, Boutros sent DePodesta emails demanding that DePodesta open FBI investigations into individuals with political views or affiliations in opposition to the Trump administration,” the complaint continues.

The suit centers on the spectacular collapse of the DoJ’s criminal case against six activists who were protesting against an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility in the Broadview suburb of Chicago in September of 2025. The activists, who became known as the Broadview Six, were charged with conspiracy to impede an ICE officer, and the case dragged on for months before prosecutors were forced to dismiss the case after a series of missteps.

A grand jury initially rejected the charges presented by federal prosecutors, an extremely rare outcome as the standard of proof is low in those proceedings, with grand juries typically bringing the indictments sought by the DoJ. Even after grand jurors had expressed skepticism about the charges after reviewing footage, prosecutors went back to the grand jury to continue to pursue an indictment, with Boutros himself appearing in court to urge charges, DePodesta’s suit says.

Boutros had publicly suggested the charges were not based on political considerations, with his office saying he had not communicated with DoJ headquarters about the case, the lawsuit says. But DePodesta said those claims were false and that he himself had sat in on two meetings where Boutros discussed the Broadview Six with DoJ officials, including one meeting with Patel and Blanche.
DePodesta’s suit suggests the US attorney’s office in particular faced pressure from the Trump administration to bring charges against Kat Abughazaleh, an activist who then was running for Congress.

A judge later found that prosecutors had engaged in misconduct in the grand jury proceedings. Boutros told the court at the time that he was “completely unaware” of the problems, but DePodesta’s suit says the US attorney did know about the misconduct and that his remarks to the judge were “intentionally false”.

After the case fell apart, Boutros faced “public humiliation”, the suit says. “To deflect attention from his own malfeasance, Boutros began a campaign within the Department of Justice to blame DePodesta for the unraveling of the case.”

“Despite knowing that the case was dismissed because of improprieties by those under Boutros’s supervision, and Boutros himself,” the suit continues, “Boutros repeatedly complained to his superiors in Washington that DePodesta was responsible for the disintegration of the Broadview Six case.”

Boutros falsely accused DePodesta of conspiring with his sister-in-law, Nancy DePodesta, to destroy the case, according to the suit. Nancy DePodesta, a defense lawyer, represented one of the Broadview Six defendants.

DePodesta told his superiors he had not discussed the case with his sister-in-law, and senior FBI officials supported him, but were ultimately pressured to force DePodesta out of his position, the suit alleges.

DePodesta, who had been with the FBI since 2002, resigned in July. At the time, the FBI, in response to a post about his departure, wrote on X.com: “Anyone who is not on board with THIS FBI under the leadership of President Trump … is free to leave.” That post, the lawsuit alleges, was a “false and defamatory explanation of his removal”.
The suit alleges defamation and violations of due process and free speech rights.
DePodesta’s attorneys did not immediately respond to inquiries.
In an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times, DePodesta said: “The American people need to know what is happening within their government … I will not let fear silence me.”
Spokespeople for the DoJ, Boutros and the FBI did not respond to inquiries.

Trump-appointed DoJ leaders across the US have faced scrutiny for pursuing weak cases that align with the president’s agenda and ultimately end in failure. Boutros’s lawsuit notes that only around 6% of cases brought by Boutros against anti-ICE protesters during Operation Midway Blitz have resulted in a finding of guilt – “an unprecedented failure rate” for his office.

articles.title: Woman, 48, and boy, 12, arrested after air cadet leader assaulted while selling poppies in Hamilton
articles.summary: The 59-year-old victim is a commanding officer and was supervising young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday. Police said the 12-year-old and another boy approached them and 'blew a loud…

image.caption: Hamilton police arrested a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman after the assault of a man selling poppies, police say. (Hamilton Police)

blocks.text: Hamilton

The 59-year-old victim is a commanding officer and was supervising young cadets selling Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday. Police said the 12-year-old and another boy approached them and 'blew a loud air horn directly into [the young cadets'] ears' and an altercation ensued.
The man suffered 'life-altering' injuries, police said
A man helping young air cadets sell poppies in Hamilton suffered "life-altering" injuries after an alleged assault by a 12-year-old boy and a 48-year-old woman, Hamilton police say.

The man, 59, is a commanding officer for the Royal Canadian Air Cadets and was supervising the selling of Remembrance Day poppies on Sunday when two boys approached them and "blew a loud air horn directly into [the young cadets'] ears," police said in a release on Monday.

They were outside a restaurant at The Centre on Barton, near Barton and Ottawa streets, at about 1:45 p.m. on Sunday. The man followed the boys into the restaurant "to confront them about their actions," police said on Monday.
According to police, "a struggle ensued" and a woman who was not initially involved started assisting the boys and assaulted the victim, causing him to fall.
One of the boys hit the victim "several times," police said, before leaving the scene. The woman also left before police arrived.
Police said when officers arrived, the man was suffering from serious injuries, which paramedics attended to before taking him to hospital.
The 12-year-old boy was arrested and charged with aggravated assault and assault level one. Police found him and the other boy later that day after reports of "a new, unrelated disturbance."
The second boy was not arrested, police say "as officers were able to see footage of the incident and determined his role/actions."
The woman was arrested Monday morning and charged with aggravated assault.
'Unsettling' seeing kids so young involved in assault

Veronica Formosa, who says she saw the aftermath of the incident, was arriving at the Mandarin restaurant at the Centre on Barton when she saw two kids running from the restaurant to Boston Pizza next door.

When she went inside the Mandarin, a hostess at the restaurant told her she couldn't be seated due to an "incident that involved a man and some youths fighting." People at the restaurant were telling her what happened when the same two kids ran back into the Mandarin and left shortly after.
Formosa said she later saw the man, who seemed to be wearing military-style clothing, being cared for by paramedics.
Formosa said the boys looked "really young."
"And to be involved in something like this, that's unsettling," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Aura Carreño Rosas is a reporter at CBC Hamilton. She's originally from Venezuela. She has extensive experience in covering stories about immigrants and migrant workers as well as interesting people with diverse journeys. You can contact her at aura.carreno.rosas@cbc.ca

As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.

articles.title: Trump unveils results of $14m reflecting pool makeover in final appeal before midterms
articles.summary:
US president shares delayed results of chaotic renovation on DC site as Americans prepare to head to the polls

Donald Trump unveiled…

blocks.text: Donald Trump unveiled the delayed results of his $14m renovation of Washington DC’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool in what is expected to be his final press conference before voters head to the polls for the midterm elections.

On the eve of a consequential election day, with polls indicating that most voters feel the US president has grown too focused on building projects in the nation’s capital, he stood in front of the newly opened reflecting pool to discuss – in detail – changes to the pool’s pipe, the grass surrounding the area and granite.
“This project should be a project that unites all Americans,” Trump told reporters on Monday afternoon.

It has proven anything but. After Trump’s first revealed his “beautiful” makeover of the reflecting pool in June, a massive algae bloom turned it green (instead of the promised “American flag blue”) and the coating started to peel away.

Trump alleged that vandals were to blame, although his administration failed to produce evidence to substantiate such claims. While former Olympic canoeist David Hearn was initially charged over alleged damage, the office of the US attorney Jeanine Pirro later dropped the case, infuriating the president.
Hearn’s attorneys said the case’s dismissal “does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong”.

On Monday, Trump accused his Democratic predecessors, Joe Biden and Barack Obama, of overspending on previous renovations to the reflecting pool and once again, without evidence, accused vandals of purposefully damaging the Trump administration’s renovations.

Roughly 20 minutes into his remarks on the reflecting pool, less than 24 hours before Americans head to the polls, Trump pivoted to acknowledge Tuesday’s midterm elections, which he declared to be crucial.
The party of a sitting president often loses seats during the midterms, he noted. “We gave this a very strong shot,” Trump said.
For weeks, polls have shown Democratic candidates are narrowly ahead of Republican candidates in key races – that includes competitive Senate races in Texas, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa and Maine.
Voters have expressed dissatisfaction with Trump’s handling of his job as president, particularly over the US economy and cost of living.

The prices of gas and groceries have risen since the beginning of the year, and inflation has remained stubbornly high – largely the result of the war with Iran that Trump started at the end of February.

articles.title: Migration is a moral issue for Burnham – but he also wants to tell a positive story
articles.summary:
While PM is keen to support those making a contribution his backing of Shabana Mahmood’s hard line is no surprise

While out on the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham

blocks.text: While out on the campaign trail in Makerfield, Andy Burnham gave a glimpse into where he might land on Labour’s plans for immigration reform, which had already been decried by the left of the party as unfair and the right as electorally necessary.

Asked by the Guardian what he thought of Reform’s attack on “open borders Andy” – Nigel Farage’s early attempt to define him as soft on migration – the then Manchester mayor dismissed the charge as “ridiculous” and went on the defensive.

“I’m not like that. You know me. I was in the Home Office under Tony Blair, and actually, it was my job to return people. That was my specific role,” he said while out knocking on doors in the constituency.

“I used to have to travel to governments around the world and persuade them to take back planes of people who had come here with no basis to stay, so you know, I’ve never have been shy of getting to grips with these difficult issues.”
But Burnham wasn’t just pitching to the Reform-inclined voters he needed to win the seat; he was already charting whatever path he might then need to take if he made it all the way to Downing Street.

While he was supportive of attempts by the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, to limit legal and illegal migration, which had been criticised by some senior Labour figures as unBritish, Burnham wanted to reframe the changes.
“I think there’s a different way of thinking about it that might in the end get you to a better position, and one that restores public confidence,” he said.

The prime minister’s political allies say he regards migration as a moral issue, showing people who’ve lost faith in politics that the government does have control over the UK’s borders and is prepared to do something about it.

But he also wants to tell a positive story about the contribution of migration to the country, they say. Weeks after arriving in No 10, the Guardian revealed that social care workers could be exempted from the plans as he looked for ways to relieve pressure on the sector.

In an interview with ITV this week, Burnham again tried to make the case. “When you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say if it’s too high or too low,” he said, arguing that migrants help plug “gaps in the economy”.
In the end, Mahmood’s reforms came with a significant carve-out for almost 300,000 care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain (ILR) after five years.

In a further compromise to those on the Labour benches feeling squeamish, those deemed to be making a “strong contribution” to the UK – high earners, those with strong British connections or who work in health and teaching – will also be able to settle in five years.

But that Burnham delivered the bulk of Mahmood’s hardline reforms should not come as a surprise to anybody who has been paying attention. The prime minister, steeped in the politics of the “red wall”, understands better than many the salience of the issue with voters.

The most rigorous of the new rules first drawn up a year ago by the Home Office – retrospective changes for many migrants or forcing small boats arrivals to face up to 30 years before applying for settlement – are still there.

How they land with the public (which polling suggests supports a doubling of the waiting time for most migrants to 10 years) now depends in part on whether ministers can convince them it’s about people making a contribution, rather than a U-turn forced by their own side.
The Conservatives and Reform, unsurprisingly, are already pushing the latter narrative, with Farage describing the care workers carve-out as “the beginning of the capitulation” on borders.

Burnham is, equally predictably, arguing that it’s about fairness. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier,” he said.
“Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”
But Burnham’s words did not come in the Commons chamber or at a press conference standing alongside Mahmood or even as part of his prolific social media output.

They were instead issued in a press release, after the government chose to push ahead with the sensitive policy announcement while he was out of the country – travelling to the Commonwealth leaders summit in Antigua.

The plans are still likely to face criticism from some on either wing of the Labour party, although plenty of former critics do now appear to be on board. But without an obvious vote to coalesce around, any rebellion looks unlikely.
Mahmood’s bigger challenge will be convincing the public. She will need Burnham, who has praised her for “gripping this problem” so is presumably fully behind them, to help her to do so.

articles.title: Snapchat reaches settlement in case after teens allege platform designed to be addictive
articles.summary: Snapchat parent Snap Inc. has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and…

image.caption: Multiple cases have been brought against social media companies alleging that they designed their products to be addictive for young people. In the latest case, Snapchat has reached a settlement over claims brought by two teenagers. (Hollie Adams/Illustration/Reuters)

blocks.text: Health·New

Snapchat parent Snap Inc. has reached a settlement during a trial over claims brought by two teenagers who say the company designed the platform to be addictive, causing their depression, anxiety and eating disorders, attorneys for the plaintiffs said on Monday.
Two teens brought forward lawsuit alleging addictive platform caused issues like depression

Jury selection began last week for the trial, the second in Los Angeles state court over claims brought by young people who say they became addicted to social media after Snap, Meta Platforms, TikTok and Alphabet's YouTube designed their platforms to encourage compulsive use.
The plaintiffs had previously settled with Meta, TikTok and YouTube.

"Our ultimate goal is to hold these social media companies accountable for how their actions have impacted millions of children across the country, and these settlements allow us to keep building toward that goal," John Morgan and Emily Jeffcott, trial attorneys for plaintiff K.D.B., said in a statement.

The trial was set to be the first for Snap in the sweeping litigation over social media's impact on teens, after the company settled the other cases that had been scheduled for trial. The company's chief executive, Evan Spiegel, had been expected to testify.

The case had been selected from thousands of pending lawsuits as a bellwether intended to test the claims against Snap and the other companies and potentially influence how similar cases are resolved. The next bellwether trials are scheduled to begin in March, according to the plaintiffs' lawyers.

Companies like Snapchat have rejected claims that their platforms are designed to be addictive. The next bellweather trials over social media's impact on teens are expected to begin in March. (Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters)

A Snap spokesperson said in a statement that the company has built safeguards, launched safety tutorials and partnered with experts, and remains committed to "continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community."

Plaintiffs S.J., a 16-year-old girl from Illinois, and K.D.B., an 18-year-old from Mississippi, say they began using YouTube as early as age 3 and the other platforms around age 9, developing compulsive habits they blame on features such as autoplay and infinite scroll.
The companies have rejected claims their platforms were designed to addict young people, and say they have taken action to make the apps safe places for young people to express themselves.
What could the Meta settlement in California mean for Canada?
Wave of lawsuits

Social media companies are facing thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts brought by individuals, school districts, municipalities and other government entities alleging the companies knowingly sought to addict children to their platforms, contributing to a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression and suicide.
Around 30 states have filed lawsuits against the companies, court records show.

items: TikTok settles landmark lawsuit over youth addiction claims
Kids and young adults are addicted to screens. New research argues it may be a public health concern
How teen accounts on Instagram and Facebook are changing after Meta's $18B US settlement

blocks.text: In the first case to go to trial, which ended in March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube had been negligent and awarded a young woman $6 million US in damages.
The next two teens whose cases were selected for trials either settled or dropped their claims against the companies.
Meta and YouTube must pay woman $6M US in addiction trial
The first school district chosen for trial settled with all of the companies.
Also in March, Meta lost both phases of a lawsuit brought by New Mexico, and was ordered to pay $375 million US after a jury found it had misled consumers about the safety of its platforms.

articles.title: Man guilty of stealing cash from farm owned by South African president
articles.summary: The case, part of the "Farmgate" scandal, has left President Cyril Ramaphosa mired in an impeachment saga.

blocks.text: A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.

David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.

David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.

The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.

In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

articles.title: Fossilised red blood cells found in 115m-year-old dinosaur’s bone, say scientists
articles.summary:
Chemical tests on Aratasaurus bone identify presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around body

It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park…

blocks.text: It could be the opening of a Jurassic Park rip-off: scientists examining ancient dinosaur bones find what appear to be fossilised red blood cells, and traces of the molecule that gives the beast’s blood its distinctive crimson hue.

But that is what researchers are claiming to have discovered after analysing the hind leg bones of a small, meat-eating dinosaur called an Aratasaurus that lived and died in what is now north-eastern Brazil 115m years ago.

Electron microscope images of the dinosaur bones revealed small, round structures that resemble red blood cells in fine channels where blood vessels once ran, while chemical tests identified the presence of heme, the organic compound that allows haemoglobin in blood to carry oxygen around the body.

Such claims are controversial because biological tissues and molecules can break down fast, leaving little or no trace in ancient fossils. But if confirmed, it would open up entirely new avenues for scientists, allowing them to investigate dinosaur blood, metabolism and even their activity levels.

“We are seeing a mineral and molecular echo of the dinosaur’s original biology,” said Prof Kliti Grice at Curtin University in Western Australia who led the research team. “Fossilised red blood cells with distinct chemistry related to heme have never been found in situ in any fossil, let alone a dinosaur. This is a world first.”

The fossilised remnants of the Aratasaurus were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil, where researchers continue to study them. While analysing the dinosaur’s hind leg bones, Grice spotted the structures that resembled red blood cells.

The scientists’ suspicions that they were looking at red blood cells were bolstered when chemical tests came back positive for heme and its breakdown products. Tests also found traces of the amino acid building blocks for collagen, a key protein in connective and other tissues.

blocks.caption: A portion the Aratasaurus’s hind limb. The remains were discovered in a mine in 2008 and have since been held in the National Museum of Brazil. Photograph: Curtin University

blocks.text: If the structures really are fossilised red blood cells, as the researchers contend, it raises the question of how they were preserved. According to Grice, a manganese compound called hausmannite, which formed in and around the blood cells, may have lent a helping hand by stabilising them prior to fossilisation. The same process might have helped preserve the amino acids, she added. The study appears in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The work is already stoking debate. Prof Mary Schweitzer at North Carolina State University in the US, who has discovered remnants of blood vessels and soft tissues in dinosaur fossils, is not convinced Grice and her colleagues have found red blood cells. One reason for her doubt is that the dinosaur’s red blood cells should have a “nuclear bulge” making them appear dome-like on both sides. The structures Grice found are concave, suggesting they might be something else.

Schweitzer was more persuaded by the discovery of heme and collagen amino acids in the bone and said there was so much more to learn from exceptionally well-preserved fossils. Schweitzer added: “The conventional wisdom in palaeontology that all endogenous organics would disappear in a million years or less is being routinely challenged, and will continue to be as technological approaches to palaeontological specimens are more routinely applied.”

Another question the research raises is what other biological material might lurk in fossils collections around the world. On this, Grice urges extreme caution, adding that her work does not imply that large biological molecules such as proteins or DNA live on in ancient fossils. “Any extraordinary claim needs extraordinary analytical evidence,” she said. “The aim isn’t to find Jurassic Park DNA, it’s to determine how much genuine molecular information deep time can preserve.”

“The really exciting implication is that extraordinary molecular information may already be sitting in museum collections around the world, waiting for us to ask new questions of old fossils,” she added.

articles.title: Copilot in deadly Florida jet crash identified in reports as 20-year-old
articles.summary: In air traffic audio, a crew member can be heard shouting: "We are going to crash into the ground!"

blocks.text: Dashcam footage captures Florida private jet crash
A 20-year-old copilot was among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in Florida on Sunday, according to US media.

Nathalia Filgueiras, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, is reported to have been one of two crew members aboard the Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed near West Palm Beach.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said it would investigate to what extent ice and turbulence may have contributed to the crash, and whether human error played a role.
One man on the ground sustained a leg injury when the aircraft nosedived on to a street near Cresthaven, nine miles (14 km) from President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort.
Images from the scene show a large fiery crater in the middle of a residential suburban street.
The debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area, officials told a news conference on Monday, possible evidence that the plane broke up before it hit the ground.
Officials describe how Learjet flight unfolded before deadly crash
The NTSB confirmed that after the jet took off from Austin, the crew transmitted to air traffic control that they were encountering ice and moderate turbulence.
"We are picking up precipitation, requesting to climb to 37,000 feet if able," the crew said.
NTSB member Tom Chapman said that less than 30 seconds later, the plane began to descend and the crew issued a mayday call.
The transmission then became "unintelligible", he said, adding that: "Sadly, all aboard were lost."
Flight analysis indicates the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.

In air traffic control audio, a crew member can be heard declaring an emergency, shouting "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".
Three years before crash, young copilot spoke of earning pilot licence
Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."
None of the other eight people on board has been identified.

blocks.caption: Map of the West Palm Beach, Florida area showing the reported flight path of an aircraft. A red line approaches from the northwest, loops south of President Donald J. Trump International Airport, and ends at a marked crash site near Palm Springs. Key locations labeled include West Palm Beach, Mar…

blocks.text: The NTSB said that ice and turbulence were factors in the crash.
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
The NTSB said determining the probable cause of the crash will be a "lengthy investigatory process".
As part of the investigation, the NTSB is working with the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), representatives from Learjet as well as meteorologists and air traffic control experts.
Recovering the wreckage from the crater on the roadway will be a "daunting challenge", said Timothy Monville, an air safety investigator with the NTSB.
He added that an individual who was in a vehicle near the crash site sustained a leg injury.
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash.

"When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference on Sunday. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy".

blocks.caption: A map shows Learjet's sudden descent.

blocks.text: The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road lined with businesses and restaurants.
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Trump was at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

articles.title: Russell Brand is not a ‘psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal’, court told
articles.summary:
Defence barrister says earlier allegations about comedian’s sexual conduct ‘poisoned the wells’ of justice as trial continues

Russell Brand is not a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks…

blocks.text: Russell Brand is not a “psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal” and is respectful when women say no, a court has heard.

In his closing speech at Southwark crown court, Brand’s barrister, Ian Winter KC, questioned why Brand’s accusers had not fought back when they were allegedly raped, saying “not one of them resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”.

Winter said allegations about the comedian’s sexual conduct in 2023 had “poisoned the wells” of justice. He also said there had been “monstrous delays” in the women in the criminal trial coming forward to police.
He also questioned why Brand had been accused of “only three rapes in 10 years” out of all the women he had slept with.

He said: “It is an extremely curious feature of this case that out of the many, many women that Mr Brand had sex with during this period only three of them say they did not consent to anal, oral or vaginal sex.”
Brand, 51, is accused of seven offences, including rape and sexual assault, against six women in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.

Winter began his closing speech by reciting an 1864 quote from the theologian and philosopher John Henry Newman, saying: “What I insist upon here, now that I am bringing this portion of my discussion to a close, is this unmanly attempt of his, in his concluding pages, to cut the ground from under my feet … this I call poisoning the wells.”

He said the 2023 reporting of sexual misconduct allegations in a Channel 4 Dispatches documentary and Times and Sunday Times stories had “poisoned the well of justice” in Brand’s case by prompting the women to come forward with accusations afterwards.
Winter told jurors: “They poisoned the wells in the hope and intention that other people come forward and make allegations against him.”

In her closing speech on Friday, the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC, denied that the 2023 reporting had had “such a subliminal hold on the minds of six perfectly rational women” to make them “invent, reimagine, recharacterise, recast” their encounters with the comedian.
Winter told jurors on Monday that Brand had an “immense amount of sex” and none of it was unlawful.
“The question for you is, can you possibly be sure in this case that out of the many, many women who voluntarily had sex with Mr Brand between 1999 and 2009, he raped just three of them?” he asked.
“Living a highly promiscuous life is entirely lawful however morally distasteful you may find it,” he continued. “Disgusting, distasteful, immoral – who cares? It’s irrelevant to your consideration.”
Winter said another “curious feature” of the case was that the three rape complainants had alleged Brand was “normal” after the alleged incidents.

“That, we suggest, is something that simply cannot have occurred if he is guilty,” the barrister said. “He obviously genuinely believed that they were consenting because that’s the only thing that would explain why his behaviour was normal.”
The barrister said there was “no evidence he is some sort of psychopath who rapes people and thinks it’s normal”.

He also questioned why the women had not screamed, kicked out or slapped Brand during the alleged attacks. He asked why a woman who accuses Brand of anal rape “didn’t just roll over and kick out in any way” and said she “didn’t scream or resist or call out”. He also questioned why a woman who says she was orally raped did not “slap [Brand] in the face” and suggested she had not “sufficiently” resisted.
He also questioned how none of the women came forward during the #MeToo movement.
Winter said: “How is it that it’s only three out of the many, many women, how is it that not even these ones, not even these allegations on this indictment came to light during #MeToo?
“Many women were questioning whether they had a bad experience sexually at the hands of a famous person. It could not have been more publicised.
“How is it that not one of them thought what happened to them involved a crime during the #MeToo movement?”

The court has heard the earliest allegation dated back to 1999, when a woman accused Brand of raping her after he had performed in a fringe cabaret event during the Labour party conference in Bournemouth.
The woman told the court Brand had left his email address after raping her, while asking her if she was enjoying herself.

Winter said the woman was not a “naive and wilting flower” as he questioned her account of events. “You would have to be a psychopath to be raping someone and asking them if they were enjoying it,” Winter said. “He [Brand] said he was trying to please her but he wasn’t successful.”
Winter said rapists did not try to please their victims. He also said Brand respected when a woman said no, and sought “approbation and adoration” from women.

“He respects it when a woman says no so that makes him someone who is not a rapist,” Winter said. “He was seeking the approval in the sex, it’s the approval, it’s the ‘Yes I will have sex with you’, and that’s what he said in his evidence.”

Brand is accused of three counts of rape and three counts of sexual assault. On Tuesday, an allegation of indecent assault was changed to a charge of attempted indecent assault. Brand has pleaded not guilty to all charges.
The trial continues.

articles.title: How a Toronto rec basketball league became a million-dollar business
articles.summary: Brodie Rec League is a basketball league that launched in Burlington in 2020 and now has 50,000 athletes playing across 25 cities in North America including Burnaby, Toronto, Brooklyn, and Boston.

image.caption: Brodie Rec League is a basketball league that launched in Burlington in 2020 and now has 50,000 athletes playing across 25 cities in North America including Manhattan, Toronto, Brooklyn, and Boston. (Submitted by Brodie Rec League)

blocks.text: Basketball
Brodie Rec League is a basketball league that launched in Burlington in 2020 and now has 50,000 athletes playing across 25 cities in North America including Burnaby, Toronto, Brooklyn, and Boston.
'It’s the closest thing you can get to a professional without actually being professional,' says CEO
Rec level basketball is nothing new, but a rec league game where the players are made to feel like professional stars? That’s something people seem to be getting behind.
For a standard $350 sign-up fee, players receive team jerseys and compete as Brodie athletes for the season.

The real difference maker is what’s available off the court. From a pre-season media day where athletes get their photos professionally taken, to player stats online, to captured video on the court for use on social media.

“It’s the closest thing you can get to a professional without actually being professional,” Brodie CEO Connor Renton said. “Most rec sports are racing to be the cheapest thing possible, and we don’t want it to be the cheapest, we want it to be the best.”
The league even holds a mid-season all-star game where players get voted into play.
Meanwhile, investors are seeing that this isn’t just another community-centre recreation league, it’s a million-dollar business opportunity.
On Sept. 29, Brodie announced it had received $5 million in funding, led by Toronto-based Golden Ventures and New York-based Lerer Hippeau.

After appearing on the Fall 2026 season of Dragon’s Den, where Renton said he plans to “build the next Nike,” the league also secured another $1.5 million at a $30-million valuation, from three investors who now own five per cent of the league.
But with private intramural sports leagues having existed for decades, what makes Brodie so appealing to investors?
Same product, just sold differently
According to the NCAA, only 0.03 per cent of college level basketball players will make it to the NBA.
With this in mind, Renton says he’s building a league for everyone else.
“We are the whole sports industry,” he says. “There's way more people on the sidelines waiting to get involved that just weren't playing.”
Investors are seeing that this isn’t just another community-centre rec league, it’s a million-dollar business opportunity. (Submitted by Brodie Rec League)

Michael Naraine, an associate professor of sport management at Brock University, says Brodie does more than just build community ties, like a traditional intramural league does and instead Brodie is offering to make its athletes feel like stars.
“What they’re selling is the, ‘Hey, you still got it,’ even though these people may have never ‘had it,’ in the first place,” Naraine said.
This distinction could help explain the “it factor” attracting investors to Brodie.
As Naraine puts it, “It's literally the same product just sold differently and at a higher premium margin that they can get better returns on.”
Content is key in 2026
One of the ways players are made to feel like stars is through online content, which, in 2026 is just as important as the product a business is selling.
The creator economy is currently valued at around $250 billion US in 2026, according to a Global Economy Report 2026.
For Brodie, content creation has been key to establishing their brand beyond the four quarters of a rec basketball game.
According to Renton, Brodie releases 15,000 pieces of content every week, from player action shots to highlight reels of big plays.
“Content is huge. It’s what grew Brodie, it’s how we were able to grow as fast as we could.
According to Renton, Brodie releases 15,000 pieces of content every week, from player action shots to highlight reels of big plays. (Submitted by Brodie Rec League)
Everyone wants to be a superstar, but no one gets consistent content,” Renton said.

He also plans to capitalize on an influencer-marketing strategy, where he’ll allow influencers to play for free in exchange for sharing Brodie content, expanding the brand’s reach and engagement online.
Eventually, the goal is to pay Brodie athletes via a monetized creator model, similar to that of how social media influencers make money.

“It’s the same way that TikTok has a creator program and YouTube pays you for monetization,” he said. “Advertisers want to advertise with us … if you're a Brodie athlete, there's no reason why you can't get paid to be.”
Experiences more attractive than ever
Pickup basketball is nothing new, but in a time where in-person connection is coveted more than ever, marketing the experience is a key factor in scaling a sports league.
In 2025, the global experiences market was valued at more than $1 trillion and is actively projected to reach $2.5 trillion by 2032, according to a report from Financial Service provider Empower.
An increased desire for in-person connection following the pandemic, as well as feelings of FOMO (fear of missing out), are reasons cited for the growth.
“Coming out of COVID what the end consumer has said time and time again is that they want to experience,” Naraine said. “Millennials in particular have disposable income.”
He adds that sports leagues currently meet two major demands: in-person experience for the young adults craving it, and a chance to compete well into their 20s and 30s.

The desire for in-person community is also part of the growth of adult sport meet-ups across North America in recent years, says Jeff Este, co-founder of New York based GoodRec, an app for pickup soccer that helps players find and join games in different cities.

Este founded the business with two friends after recognizing how challenging it was to organize pick-up games around schedules. The goal was to make playing as easy as ordering take-out food: find a game nearby and show up.

“There’s kind of this shadow market of people who, if you can find a very convenient, well-run game, that there isn’t this huge commitment … we feel like there's a huge market to be serviced” Este says, in reference to adults who stopped playing sports as they got older.
GoodRec now operates across multiple North American cities, with Toronto being the app’s most popular market with about 35 games a day.
“There’s a lot of people searching for a place,” he says. “That thirst for community and playing together and a reason to come together … sports is perfect.”
Where to from here?
With an influx of $6.5 million (CAD) cash and an expansion into more cities across North America, Brodie finds itself in a pivotal moment of the business.
Renton says the league's current primary revenue source is player registrations but sees future potential in sponsorships and media deals.
“As soon as we start stacking sponsorship deals and TV media deals and all these other things, my goal is to make Brodie as cheap as possible,” he says.

Renton adds that the money he raised will go into two buckets: better infrastructure for the game time experience at gyms, and an improved user-experience on the app where the content and player stats live.
“Brody has given the 99.9 per cent of athletes not only a third place, but also a second life.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Tara is a Toronto-based journalist who writes and produces athlete features for CBC Sports, exploring the intersection of sport, society, and culture. Prior to this, she was a writer for the CTV News national editorial team, covering trending and breaking news. Tara's bylines have appeared in Toronto Life, Canadian Business, and Maclean’s where she covers stories related to culture, entertainment, and sports. She holds a Master’s degree from Toronto Metropolitan University.

articles.title: Trump to remove Rwanda and South Africa from US trade deal
articles.summary: The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by the US Treasury.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

articles.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California midterm ballots
articles.summary: The Trump administration has appealed to the Supreme Court over claims that a list of more than 20,000 ballots in California include non-US citizens. Multiple courts and independent analysis have…

image.caption: Early voting has been underway in California since October Image: Mario Tama/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: On the eve of the US midterm elections, the administration of President Donald Trump is making a last ditch attempt to sideline over 20,000 mail in ballots in California, claiming non-US citizens are attempting to vote.

The US Justice Department (DoJ), which is run by Trump's former personal attorney Todd Blanche, claims to have a list documenting non-US citizens on California's voter rolls. In mid October, the federal government first filed a lawsuit based on the allegations.
A district court judge rejected the DoJ request, warning that singling out ballots would "wreak havoc" on the election process and harm voters' trust in the democratic process.

"If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote Los Angeles District Judge David Carter in rejecting the Trump administration's initial lawsuit in October.
Battle for US midterm elections heats up

In bringing its case to the Supreme Court on Monday, the DoJ asked for a "limited injunction" directing the state of California to "stop commingling suspected illegal ballots with legal ones" pending the verification of voters' status.
Early voting has been underway in California for several weeks, with hundreds of thousands of ballots already processed.
It is unclear if the Supreme Court will respond in time for a ruling to have an effect on tomorrow's election.
Analysis shows thousands of eligible voters on ballot blacklist

The voter list had been compiled by the US Department of Homeland Security. In its response to the federal government's lawsuit, California defended its election integrity, and said the process used by the Trump administration to identify non-citizen voters was likely flawed and full of errors.
Last week, another federal judge ordered the DoJ to share its list with an immigrant rights group, and a voting rights watchdog based out of the University of California Los Angeles (UCLA).

A legal filing of the analysis found that thousands of US citizens on the list appear to be inexplicably flagged as ineligible to vote. US District Judge Carter said people recently flagged as noncitizens on voter rolls in other states have repeatedly turned out to be naturalised US citizens.
Trump's fixation on voter fraud
Trump has made unfounded claims of election fraud for years, despite multiple investigations finding such malfeasance is exceedingly rare.
For the current midterm election cycle, Trump has zeroed in on claiming non US citizens are trying to vote, despite these claims being repeatedly debunked by research and investigation.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own ​constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," US District Judge Carter wrote in October.
The most populous US state, California, leans heavily Democratic, and is not expected to be a competitive state for Trump's Republicans in the midterms.
California governor Gavin Newsom is an outspoken critic of Trump, and has warned the president's administration against trying to interfere in the state's voting process.

Ahead of the midterm voting on Tuesday, Newsom announced the deployment of election law experts, poll observers and a help line for voters to report any attempts of intimidation or interference at the polls.
