articles.title: Legal challenge to Australia's social media ban to start in High Court
articles.summary: A rights group will argue the world-leading policy robs under-16s of their right to free communication.

blocks.text: Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.

In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.

The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."
"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.

Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, £52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.

articles.title: Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why?
articles.summary: After a second apparent cyber-attack in as many weeks, we examine possible culprits and their motives

blocks.text: Supermarket fridges and freezers in seven European countries have malfunctioned, their thermostats remotely cranked up in some cases to 50C (122F).
The EU has condemned what it said was “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”.

blocks.caption: Workers at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, dispose of spoiled food.  Photograph: Johan Nilsson/EPA

blocks.text: Which supermarkets were affected and what does it mean?
The attack hit fridges in Belgian branches of Carrefour, Intermarché and Ikea, Coop and ICA in Sweden, Delhaize in Luxembourg, Kesko in Finland, SupaValu in Ireland and shops in Estonia.

It appeared to be a reprise of attacks three weeks ago when French retailers had to ditch huge amounts of food when their fridges suddenly overheated as a result of anonymous hackers seizing control of their internet-exposed appliance management software.

Something similar may have happened in the US in early August when a series of mysterious fridge malfunctions hit commissaries at least six military bases. The Pentagon is investigating a suspected hack.

This is feared to signal a new front in cyber-attack and hacking tactics. Fridges are not unique in having their controls exposed to hackers. Many ovens, washing machines, dishwashers and central heating systems are linked to the internet to allow remote access and automated control.
Who is doing it?

No politically motivated “hacktivist” group has claimed responsibility and neither has a ransomware gang exploited the vulnerability to demand the supermarkets pay - which in any event would be difficult because the damage is already done when their fridges overheat.

“The two most plausible attribution scenarios for me are some kind of state-based signalling and demonstration of capability or some kind of lone-wolf hacker that is conducting these attacks for their own personal reasons,” said Rafe Pilling, the senior director for threat intelligence at the cybersecurity company Sophos.

The state-linked actor theory seems most likely, in part because of the obvious psychological impact on large populations of seeing food stripped from shelves. North Korea is believed to have been behind last week’s Binance cryptocurrency heist, but in this case hackers linked to Russia and China are also likely to be in the frame.
Western intelligence chiefs say Moscow is waging a campaign of sabotage in Europe that takes many different forms and is likely to intensify in the coming months.

blocks.caption: A worker at a branch of ICA in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, disposes of spoiled food. Photograph: Johan Nilsson/TT/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Discerning the culprit is made harder by the relative simplicity of the hack. No malware was needed, which means there is no trace of a weapon at the scene of the crime. Pilling compared it to “wearing rubber gloves and messing with the switches”.
How is it possible?

The software that manages commercial fridges is connected to the internet, which means lines of code can be left vulnerable to hackers. Unlike desktop or mobile devices, on which users and IT managers are often alerted to the need to install updates that contain patches to repair constantly emerging vulnerabilities, the software in items such as fridges can be left for long periods without updates.

Nick Jackson, the director of cyber-operations at the cybersecurity company Bitdefender, said one reason companies might move slowly to install patches is they can take time to run, which leaves periods when machinery needs to be offline - an obvious problem for food retailers. But he said a simpler explanation could be that the people running the fridges are not aware of the problem, “don’t think about that and it’s not top of their agenda”.

In Monday’s wave of incidents, Coop in Sweden said some of its fridges were linked to a 4G mobile network that made them more exposed. ICA said its system was provided by Danfoss, the Danish company that had problems in France.
What can shops do to defend themselves?

The simple answer is to patch their software systems. According to the Belgian refrigerator group Sabcobel, the impact of Monday’s hack could have been far worse if they had not started patching fridges after the 12 October attack in France.

In the UK, which has not yet been affected, retailers are “currently working with the National Cyber Security Centre(NSCC) to ensure their fridges and freezers are secure as possible against potential attacks” said Graham Wynn, the assistant director of regulatory affairs at the British Retail Consortium.
Why have British supermarkets not been hit yet?
Internet-exposed refrigeration systems are most popular in countries including France, Italy, Greece and Belgium, according to the cybersecurity company Forescout.

Daniel dos Santos, its vice president of research, said: “When we checked the data for these exposed systems online of supermarkets, the UK is not in the top 10.” He said the risk was not negligible, but “I wouldn’t say it’s super-high right now for the UK specifically”.
A spokesperson for the NCSC said it is “working with its international partners and industry to fully understand details of an incident”.

articles.title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash
articles.summary:
Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years

Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most…

blocks.text: Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade.
Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.

But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement.
The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”.
But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement.

She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.”

In particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes.
The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”.

Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them.

Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.”

The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal.

blocks.caption: Diane Abbott, the Labour MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington, criticised the retrospective changes. Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”.

She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.”
Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years.

Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element.

“People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.”

But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International.

The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement.
after newsletter promotion

Under pressure from health unions to make an exception for care workers, the home secretary has moved to allow an estimated 280,000 care workers and their dependents to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years.
In the revised set of proposals, care workers earning more than £25,000 will be able to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years, a third of the time that was announced last year.

blocks.caption: Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, said Mahmood’s decision would cost the country up to £10bn.  Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: Home Office officials calculate that about 500,000 migrants will have to wait longer than the current five years. But critics of Mahmood’s softening point out that 1.4 million out of the 1.9 million migrants who came to Britain under the so-called “Boriswave” surge in legal migrants will still be eligible for indefinite leave after five years.

Highest earners – those earning more than £125,000 – will be able to settle within three years. Those earning more than £50,271 and some public service workers such as doctors, nurses and teachers will be able to settle after five years.

The exception will be the small number of refugees who enter through designated safe and legal routes such as the reopening of the scheme for Afghan women and girls and Palestinians. No other refugees will be eligible for settlement if they have accessed any public funds.

Mahmood met union general secretaries to map out the changes on Monday morning, before presenting them to MPs. The Unison general secretary, Andrea Egan, said it was welcome that Mahmood had not implemented her original plans, which were “morally bankrupt and a threat to public services”.

Egan said the obligations placed on care workers to qualify for the five-year path were still onerous. “The government must make sure it isn’t unjustly denied to them. Thousands of migrant care workers have had their employment patterns and pay disrupted by rogue employers,” she said. “The power of employers to threaten workers with deportation or disrupt their route to settlement must end.”

blocks.caption: Edward Leigh, the MP for Gainsborough, was among the Conservatives who acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed legal migration numbers to rise so significantly.  Photograph: House of Commons/PA

blocks.text: Business groups warned that the retrospective nature of the changes would still cause far-reaching damage in some sectors. The CBI said the exemption for some care workers meant the policy risked “being higher costs for the relatively small number of businesses using skilled worker visas, without addressing the problem the policy was originally designed to solve”.

Make UK said it would make it far more difficult for businesses to retain skilled workers and industries would “undoubtedly lose talent to countries that welcome skilled workers rather than moving the goalposts”.

The shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, said Mahmood’s decision to allow a carve-out for care workers who arrived on the visa before May 2025 would cost the country up to £10bn, a figure Mahmood has cited in support of her original plans. The home secretary said the longer wait for settlement for more than half a million people would mean a cut to the projected benefits bill.

Other Conservative MPs acknowledged that it was the previous government who had allowed numbers to rise so significantly. The backbencher Edward Leigh said to Philp that “anybody who was serving as a Home Office minister at that time should wear sackcloth and ashes”.

articles.title: Fake nuclear warning from hacked app sparks unease but not panic in Ukraine
articles.summary: Many Ukrainians, who have faced years of Russian attacks, did not take the messages seriously and doubted their veracity.

blocks.text: Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.

On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note – a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.
But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.
Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.
"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."
"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."
The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.

Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.
Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.
"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."
"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."
There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.

Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.
"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."

While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.
Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.

"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."
Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.

"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."

The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

articles.title: Trump administration ramps up midterm battles, asks Supreme Court to intervene in California case
articles.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump's Justice Department has shown a willingness to intervene directly in Tuesday's midterm elections, raising fears its law enforcement powers are being used in a partisan…

blocks.text: What happens to Trump if the Democrats crush the midterms

U.S. President Donald Trump's Justice Department has shown a willingness to intervene directly in Tuesday's midterm elections before polls have closed, breaking with decades of practice meant to avoid the appearance that its law enforcement powers are being used in a partisan manner.

In California, the Justice Department seeks to set aside mail-in ballots from about 20,000 voters it alleges are likely non-U.S. citizens ineligible to vote. The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots from those voters.

It is one of two cases which underscore the department's willingness to intervene in election ​disputes before votes are counted. The cases have raised concerns among Democrats that, after polls close Tuesday, there will be an effort to sow doubt about the midterms, as Trump did with baseless claims of fraud following his 2020 election loss to Joe Biden, culminating in the Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the Capitol.
Voters enter the C. Blythe Andrews Jr. Public Library to cast their ballots on the final day of early voting for midterm elections in Tampa, Fla., on Sunday. (Octavio Jones/The Associated Press)
Outside groups aligned with Trump filed more than 60 lawsuits challenging his 2020 defeat, all of which ⁠were unsuccessful.

"The right-wing fringe outside groups are not going to have to do that this year because the [Justice Department] is clearly standing ready and willing to do it," said Elisabeth Frost, a voting rights lawyer with Elias Law Group, which frequently represents Democrats in court.

items: Economic frustration set to boil over in midterm elections
Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?

blocks.text: The House and Senate, which Republicans currently control by slim margins, could change hands if Democrats manage to pick up a net four seats in each chamber. All 435 House seats are up for election in the midterms, while only about one-third of the Senate's 100 seats are.
California, with 52 House of Representatives seats, can take weeks to count ballots and some of Tuesday's midterm races could be subjected to recounts and court challenges.

"Those within the recount or contest margin of error — the candidates, outside groups and the administration — will fight those tooth and nail," said Victoria Bassetti, senior adviser at States United Democracy Center, a non-profit group focused on protecting free, fair and secure elections.
LISTEN | The CBC's Jonathan Montpetit on what Trump might protest:
Day 69:26How will Trump’s voter fraud claims affect the midterms?
Data analysts question government's list

The U.S. Constitution ​assigns the responsibility of administering elections to states, though the federal government has some oversight to protect against discriminatory and other illegal practices at the state and local level.
In the California case, U.S. District Judge David Carter slammed the administration's efforts in denying its request on Oct. 28.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch," he said.
What would a U.S. midterms win look like for Democrats and Republicans? | Hanomansing Live
The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals also refused on Friday to block the ballots.

California has said that the state's safeguards against non-citizen voting are robust. As well, because the list originated from the Department of Homeland Security, state officials and immigrant rights groups fear it is being used as a pretext for contentious deportation efforts.

Multiple studies and state audits show that ineligible voting, including by non-citizens, is rare. When it occurs, it is disparate and not, to date, part of an organized effort that could sway a particular race.

An outside analysis of the list compiled by the Department of Justice has raised troubling questions. More than four in 10 names flagged as possible non-citizen voters in California by the Trump administration cannot be found on the state's voter rolls, said two data analysis members of UCLA's Voting Rights Project, who filed a lawsuit challenging it, along with the Los Angeles-based Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA).

items: Canadians caught up in Trump voter fraud crackdown as U.S. accuses Canada of election interference
5 reasons why the Democrats might not take control of Congress in U.S. midterms

blocks.text: The research found that 8,880 of the names, representing 42 per cent of the entire list, do not correspond to anyone in California's current voter file.

"The expert analysis further makes clear that the mandated voter list endangers a significant number of eligible California voters," said the filing, which was cosigned by Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for California governor and an adviser to the UCLA Voting Rights Project.
The analysis also found that thousands of U.S. citizens appear to be flagged as ineligible to vote on the government's list.
Alaska setback for Trump administration

The administration has taken an increasingly aggressive approach ​toward how states run elections. The Justice Department has told ⁠election officials in all 50 states that they could face criminal prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to remain on their rolls or cast ballots.
It has lost a series of lawsuits seeking to obtain voter rolls, including sensitive personal information, from dozens of states.
Trump slams Democrats for Alaska's double Dan Sullivan drama
The Trump administration has also vowed to appeal a ruling in Alaska.

Alaska has become a particularly intense legal battleground after the New York Times reported that Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign was involved in recruiting retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan to challenge Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

The Justice Department lawsuit, which Trump said he directed the department to file, asked a court to halt certification and order an investigation if the margin suggested voter confusion could have affected the outcome.
U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason, in Anchorage, dismissed the case on Sunday, finding ​Alaska could not conduct such a probe while preserving the secrecy of ballots.

items: Dirty tricks or much ado about nothing? Why Alaska, for once, is front and centre in midterms
Canada is in the U.S. midterm spotlight. Will the results be a blessing or a curse?

blocks.text: The lawsuit marks a rare federal intervention in the voting process and signalled a willingness by the administration to contest the election results in court.

Separate from the election result, the Justice Department has vowed to investigate whether any laws were broken in the effort that saw the politically inexperienced Dan Sullivan qualify for the ballot.

The administration already sought to restrict voting by mail for this year's midterms — a mode of casting ​ballots used more often by Democratic-leaning voters — but the Supreme Court in September rebuffed that effort.
According to an NBC News tracker, more than 24 million mail-in ballots have been cast so far, as of Monday.

articles.title: If hackers can take control of a supermarket freezer, how vulnerable is other tech?
articles.summary: Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.

blocks.text: Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.

Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.

Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.

Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

articles.title: French pupils resume school blockades as country braces for more protests
articles.summary:
Minister warns weeks without lessons are putting exams at risk as unions plan nationwide strike on Thursday

Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the…

blocks.text: Dozens of high schools across France were blockaded again on Monday as the government braced for another tense week of protests over school conditions and the high cost of living.
The protests come amid warnings that weeks without lessons are putting some pupils’ school year and final exams at risk.

As children returned after the two-week school holiday, students’ unions ignored Emmanuel Macron’s call to end the lycée blockades, which have been running since September and have prompted one of the biggest protest movements and social crises of his presidency.

From early morning in Paris and its suburbs, as well as in cities including Lille, Toulouse and Marseille, schoolchildren demanding more replacement teachers and repairs to buildings barricaded school entrances with wheelie bins. Police officers outside some schools attempted to drag the bins away and made arrests.

blocks.caption: Students gather outside a blockaded high school in Paris to protest against a lack of resources. Photograph: Nicolas Garriga/AP

blocks.text: University students’ unions were planning additional barricades at faculties on Tuesday. Trade unions have called for a large-scale strike on Thursday, with rail workers, teachers and private-sector employees planning to join demonstrations in cities across France to support schoolchildren’s demands for better conditions and protest against the rising cost of living and low salaries.

Nathanaël Combary from the school students’ union Renouveau Lycéen, who is also a member of Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, said schoolchildren must keep going in their “battle of strength” with the government to push for more funding, better access to higher education and repairs to decrepit schools.

He said measures offered by the government last week to cap some class sizes and review the university applications platform were inadequate. Combary told BFMTV that protests were the only way for schoolchildren to push a government response. He said: “Democratically speaking it’s a bit scandalous that we have to reach this type of situation to be heard but it’s the only solution we have.”

The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said he feared the school year was now “at risk” for many students in their final years who had missed weeks of classes because of the blockades and would be unable to complete coursework or catch up on the curriculum for exams.

He said: “We have pupils who are sitting their baccalauréat at the end of the year who for hundreds of thousands of them have had no classes for four or five weeks if you include holidays, and for whom the school year is now at risk. And that’s something that we can’t allow.”
Geffray said the school blockades were “illegal” and his priority was for children to return to class.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A protester adds a bin to a fire outside the Montebello international high school in Lille. Photograph: François Lo Presti/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: In Montpellier, the Socialist senator Hussein Bourgi accused the government of “misconduct” and “provocation” after video footage showed a 53-year-old school nurse saying something to police near a school barricade before being forced face-down to the ground, handcuffed and taken into police custody. The local prefect, in charge of police operations, defended the arrest, saying the woman had insulted officers and resisted police.
The education ministry said 41 high schools were blocked across France – around 1% of the nationwide total. Students’ unions put the figure at 150.

Nicolas Bonnet, of the headteachers’ union SNPDEN-UNSA, said: “It’s time for us to return to our job: teaching and supporting pupils.” He warned that coursework, final-year exams and university applications were at risk.
He said he understood why high-school students felt the government had not offered enough to fix problems in schools, but urged more dialogue between the government and pupils.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said he would meet school students’ unions again next week.

articles.title: France: Petition to ban TV channel gets 500,000 signatures
articles.summary: Support for the petition has surged since last month's shooting of a Black man by a reported avid viewer of CNews. Critics say the channel, often compared to Fox News, is a platform for…

image.caption: 'The extreme-right kills! CNews culpable!' reads this placard during a tribute to a man shot dead near Paris last monthImage: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

blocks.text: A petition urging the French government to ban a television news channel known for its hard line on immigration and crime has accrued more than 500,000 signatures amid accusations that its sensationalist coverage contributed to the racist killing of a Black man.
The petition to shut down CNews was launched in June, but support spiked after a Frenchman of Congolese origin was killed in a racially motivated attack in the Paris suburbs on October 23.

A 39-year-old man has been charged with murder and attempted murder over the incident in the commuter towns of Trappes and La Verriere west of Paris in which he said he was "targeting individuals who appeared to be Muslim, African, or North African," a prosecutor has said.
France: What is CNews?

French media have reported that the suspect was an avid consumer of CNews, which has been described as a French version of Fox News and criticized for giving too much airtime to anti-immigrant rhetoric.

The petition to "remove CNews from French broadcasting" argues that the channel, which is owned ​by conservative French billionaire Vincent Bollore, is not an ​information channel but a"propaganda machine."
Critics have claimed that CNews' broadcasting increasingly mimics lines taken by ​Le Pen's far-right National Rally (RN), which is leading in polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
Le Pen has promised to privatize public broadcasting in France, a policy from which CNews would stand to benefit.
At a rally in the northern Paris suburb of Aubervilliers last week, protesters held up posters reading slogans such as "CNews kills."
During nationwide cost-of-living protests on October 17, protesters threw projectiles and broke windows at the channel's Paris headquarters.
Meanwhile, two Green lawmakers have urged France's lower house of parliament to withdraw accreditation for CNews to protect "democracy" from "racist hatred."
Earlier this year, France expelled Russian news pundit Xenia Fedorova, who had been accused of peddling Kremlin propaganda on CNews.
Le Pen launches presidential campaign amid unrest in France
CNews refuses to comment on 'political petition'

The channel has also been accused of broadcasting racist comments about Bally Bagayoko, a Frenchman of Malian descent who is the mayor of Paris' largest suburb, Saint-Denis, and who has gained prominence for his role in defending students in his constituency against police violence during recent protests.

CNews, which has previously denied allegations it promotes far-right views and racist tropes, saying it defends freedom of expression, told the French AFP news agency it would not comment on a "political petition."
At its launch in 2017, CNews had just a 1% market share but last year became France's most-watched free-to-air news channel.
Under National Assembly rules, a ⁠public ​debate can be organized in parliament ​if a petition attracts at least 500,000 signatures.
However, a parliamentary commission must ​ first review the petition and decide whether a debate can take place.

articles.title: Russian bombing kills 18 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
articles.summary: Local officials say 27 people are missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit a village in southern Ukraine.

blocks.text: At least 18 people waiting to receive humanitarian aid in a Ukrainian village have been killed in a Russian attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".

Five people were injured and another 27 are still missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescue teams searching through the rubble.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week," the Ukrainian president wrote in a post on social media.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."

He said that after a recent a successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Meanwhile, Semikin said rescue teams were working at the scene, confirming "people were still under the rubble".
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

articles.title: Another cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps Europe, leaving food spoiled
articles.summary: The incident comes after a very similar cyberattack last month that sent fridge temperatures in some French supermarkets way up. While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, they have…

image.caption: Empty refrigeration shelves are seen inside a Delhaize Shop & Go store in Linkebeek, near Brussels, Belgium, on Monday after an overnight IT incident affected cooling and freezer systems in a number of European grocery stores. (Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

The incident comes after a very similar cyberattack last month that sent fridge temperatures in some French supermarkets way up. While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, they have heightened ​concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure, especially in the food system.
Incident comes after a similar attack on supermarket fridges in France last month

A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar ‌attack in France last month.

The attack, which raised temperatures in refrigerator and freezer units at dozens of stores, hit supermarket groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium and Luxembourg, as well as Swedish grocers ICA and Coop. Furniture-to-meatballs retailer Ikea also saw at least one store affected.

"Everything is destroyed," Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters during a visit to the store on Monday, adding the attack occurred at 2 a.m., but was only noticed hours later.
"There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees [Celsius]."
A ​spokesperson for privately held ICA said the company was aware that a "limited number of stores were affected by ​an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems."

The latest incidents follow an attack in France last month when police said hackers seized control of cooling units at hundreds of supermarkets, causing fires and food losses. Ahold Delhaize also reported a cybersecurity incident to police last month.
A notice informing customers that refrigerators are temporarily out of service is displayed on an empty case at the Delhaize Shop & Go store in Linkebeek, Belgium. (Stephanie Lecocq/Reuters)

While no one has claimed responsibility for either attack, the incidents have heightened ​concerns among European authorities about hybrid threats to infrastructure amid growing security tensions since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in sabotage or hybrid warfare operations. ⁠Reuters could not establish who was behind Monday's attacks ⁠or whether they were linked to the incidents in France.

"It is not known who is behind this attack, ‌and it may never be determined," said Katrien Eggers, spokesperson for Belgium's Centre for Cybersecurity, adding she was concerned about the growing number of incidents, in part due to AI.
"All IT systems are potentially vulnerable, and AI can now be used to successfully exploit these weaknesses — especially by sophisticated actors," she said.
'Retail is an easy target'

From refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras and alarms, an expanding range of devices, once largely mechanical, are now connected to the internet and can now be monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals.

At least some of the refrigerator units affected on Monday used ⁠temperature control technology from Danish firm Danfoss that was also targeted in the French attack. The firm said it had been working with customers to implement fixes.
During last month's French attack, Danfoss said the affected refrigeration units were running "outdated firmware," or had "reached end of life and no longer receive software or security updates."

After a cybersecurity firm detailed a potential vulnerability in Danfoss's systems over the summer that could allow hackers to gain access to the fridges and change their temperatures remotely, the company released a patch and urged customers to install it.

items: A fridge hack spoiled food in hundreds of French supermarkets. Cybersecurity experts say it's a wake-up call

blocks.text: It wasn't the first time the food system had been targeted by hackers, cybersecurity analyst Ritesh Kotak told CBC News last month. In 2021, meat supplier JBS was hit by a cyberattack that temporarily shut down operations in Canada, the U.S. and Australia. And a 2025 attack on United Natural Foods Inc. led to shortages at many Whole Foods stores.
"This is something that, unfortunately, we're going to see more of," Kotak said, adding that the situation in France should serve as a "wake-up call" that such attacks need to be taken seriously.

Boxes of spoiled food are seen outside an Intermarche supermarket in Paris on Oct. 13, the day after a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at French supermarket chains, causing food losses and fires at several stores. (Lucien Libert/Reuters)
The European Commission said the latest incidents highlight how digital threats are becoming increasingly disruptive.

"They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers' confidence in it — a warning that we must take seriously," said EU commissioner for agriculture Christophe Hansen. "The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply ‌concerning."
A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, said five shops had their fridge systems attacked.
In Ireland, wholesaler Musgrave said the incident affected systems in 13 of its SuperValu stores, forcing it to remove some chilled and frozen products from sale.

Tom Hegel, a researcher at cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, said such attacks are typically linked to extortion, political motives or nation-state operations, with the absence of financial demands in recent cases pointing ​instead to sabotage.

"Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear," he said, adding it was hard to trace hackers targeting such systems.
"An attacker who logs into an exposed control panel leaves almost nothing behind ... ⁠A teenager and an intelligence service would look much the same from the defender's side."
AI can make cyberattacks faster and smarter
Grocers tossing thousands of dollars worth of food

Carrefour, which was badly hit in last month's French attack, said 15 of its 700 stores in Belgium were affected. ⁠Ikea said one store in Belgium had been impacted and that it could not rule out disruptions at other locations.

Privately held Swedish grocery chain Coop said that seven of its 800 stores were ⁠affected by ⁠a cyber incident involving unauthorized tampering with its refrigeration systems. It said Danfoss was ​among its suppliers.

Luc De Laet, founder and owner of Belgian butchery chain De Laet & Van Haver, said he was woken at 3:30 a.m. by an employee telling him there was a problem. He rushed to his ​store south of Antwerp and found the fridges turned up as ⁠high as 18 C.
PHP flaw: How AI just hacked an unhackable part of the internet | About That
He estimated the incident ruined about €15,000 ($23,485 Cdn) worth of meat.

"It's very scary. They are hacking the system that is doing the registration of the temperature, and they can program it at a distance," he told Reuters, adding that it was infuriating to throw away so much food.
De Laet said he believed the hackers were trying to destabilize European economies. He had contacted police but did not know whether an investigation had been launched.
"I only have two words for them: Wake up, please, because there's something going on," he said.
With files from the CBC's Abby Hughes

articles.title: Trial of nine men accused of abusing woman drugged and raped by husband begins
articles.summary:
The husband, who cannot be named to protect his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences carried out at the couple’s Stockport home

Nine men have gone on trial accused of…
articles.byline: Hannah Al-Othman North of England Correspondent

blocks.text: Nine men have gone on trial accused of being involved in the abuse of a woman who was drugged, raped and sexually assaulted by her husband while he “lived a double life masked in respectability”.
The husband, who cannot be named in order to protect the anonymity of his victim, has already pleaded guilty to a number of offences against his wife spanning more than two decades.
The offences involving the nine men on trial, who the prosecution say “were [also] leading double lives”, are alleged to have taken place between 2015 and the husband’s arrest in 2025.

Two of the men, Daniel Rayner, 42, from Whitstable in Kent and David Graves, 59, from Ilkeston in Derbyshire, were described in court as “non-contact offenders”, who are alleged to have encouraged the abuse online.
The other seven were described as “contact offenders”, who are alleged to have visited the couple’s home in Stockport, Greater Manchester, and participated in the abuse of the victim.

They are Philip Wild, 58, from Stockport; Jordan Wallace, 31, from Manchester; Alan Keelan, 42, from Manchester; Jonathan Kirk, 43, from Stockport; Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport; Mohammed Sabir, 28, of no fixed abode; and Richard Townsend, 37, from Heywood in Greater Manchester.

Three other men, Sean Peers, 38, from Stockport; Keith Fotheringham, 59, from Dundee; and Graham Brougham, 74, from Northwich in Cheshire, have already admitted to abusing the woman at previous hearings at Manchester Minshull Street crown court.
Last week, Karl Lindsay, 56, from Somerset also pleaded guilty to “non-contact” offences at a hearing at the same court on Friday.

Opening the crown’s case, prosecutor Louise Oakley KC said: “Unbeknownst to [the victim], for over 20 years, her husband had been abusing her sexually in a variety of ways whilst she was asleep or was unconscious.”

Oakley said he had done so “initially taking advantage of occasions when she had drunk enough alcohol herself to put her into a deep sleep, but also on many more occasions, more and more frequently, over that 20-year period, deliberately using a cocktail of stupefying drugs, which he administered to her without her knowledge, with or without alcohol”.

Oakley said that “from 2023 onwards at the latest, though he had been talking about it for much longer, [the husband] began actively inviting other men round to their home, and, whilst his wife lay unconscious in their bed, he filmed himself and others raping and sexually abusing her”.

“They were well aware, the prosecution say, that [she] was not conscious, that is why they were there, to use her body whilst she was unaware, just as [her husband] had been doing over the preceding years.”
Oakley said the men “derived sexual gratification and enjoyment from knowing” that the victim was “unaware” or “out of it”.

The victim “had absolutely no idea it was going on”, Oakley said, “that is, until the police came round to her door and identified to her that she had been the subject of the videos” her husband had taken.
As the prosecution set out their case in court, a relative of the victim, who was in the courtroom, cried and held their head in their hands, as they were comforted by two companions.

Oakley said that while during the course of the trial it maybe be suggested that the victim was “in fact only pretending to be asleep or unconscious as part of a fantasy role play with her husband … the prosecution says that is a smokescreen”.
“What these men did”, Oakley said, “was not participation in unconventional, but consensual sexual practices: in this case it was rape and sexual assault, pure and simple.”
The court heard that the husband’s offending was discovered after undercover journalists infiltrated a chat on the Telegram messaging platform. He was arrested and his mobile phone was seized.
“That telephone was like a confession booth,” Oakley said, adding that it “contained decades’ worth of material” from other devices and cameras.
“That description cannot be underestimated,” she said. “It contained [the husband’s] darkest secrets and the barbaric sexual fantasies that he had sought to fulfil going back in time to 2004.”
She said the mobile phone contained “over a million photographs and videos, cataloguing not only his abuse of [his wife] but abuse committed by others on her, including those in the dock today”.
Oakley said the husband had “lived a double life masked in respectability” and that the nine men on trial were also “leading double lives”.

They were, she said, “either creeping in and out of [the marital home] in the hours of darkness, quietly and carefully so that they weren’t seen or heard, or hiding behind the screens of their mobile telephones and computers. No doubt believing they were safe.”
The men deny all of the charges against them. The trial at Minshull Street crown court continues.

articles.title: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack
articles.summary: Dozens of supermarkets in seven European countries dumped huge quantities of food after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.

blocks.text: In dozens of supermarkets across several European countries, a huge amount of food has been dumped after refrigerators and freezers were targeted in a cyber-attack.
Belgium and Luxemburg saw some of the worst damage, with 40 Delhaize supermarkets affected, and incidents also took place in stores across Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland.

In a branch of supermarket Delhaize in Hoeilaart, just outside the Belgian capital Brussels, the BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake found frozen pizzas and ice cream among a mountain of food having to be scrapped. This branch estimated the cost of the damage running to more than €100,000 (£83,500).

articles.title: Fighting returns to Kherson region after longest Ukraine war ceasefire
articles.summary: Though unprecedented, the six-day truce has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that continues to grinds on.

blocks.text: ByLaura Gozzi and Vitaly ShevchenkoChief analyst, BBC Monitoring
Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.

The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.

On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.

"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.

An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.

In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" – a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.

The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."

Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.

There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.

As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

blocks.text: He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling ⁠more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from ⁠cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

articles.title: Nathan Fielder lookalike contest coming to Toronto this month
articles.summary: Nathan Fielder lookalikes will compete with mock business pitches and karaoke at Toronto’s Paradise Theatre on Nov. 17.

image.caption: Nathan Fielder, pictured in Los Angeles in April 2025, has inspired lookalike contests following the success of You Can See Everything. Toronto’s Paradise Theatre will host its own competition on Nov. 17. (Michael Buckner/Variety via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment
Nathan Fielder lookalikes will compete with mock business pitches and karaoke at Toronto’s Paradise Theatre on Nov. 17.
Contestants will pitch, sing and compete at Paradise Theatre on Nov. 17
A roomful of Nathan Fielders will take over Toronto's Paradise Theatre this month as part of a lookalike competition for the Canadian comedian, actor and filmmaker.
The roughly hour-long contest will take place at the multi-arts venue on Tuesday, Nov. 17, beginning at 8 p.m. ET.

Organizers say competitors may be asked to deliver mock business pitches or take part in "Nathan-inspired karaoke," including tracks by Evanescence and Lana Del Rey — a fitting nod to a viral video posted to YouTube 12 years ago, in which Fielder sings Del Rey’s breakthrough hit, Born To Die.
Toronto comedians Andrew Phung, known for Kim's Convenience and Run the Burbs, and Hannah Spear, a Second City alumna and actor, are set to co-host and judge.
The poster for the Nathan Fielder lookalike competition, which will take place on Nov. 17 in Toronto. (Mubi, Bad Dog Theatre Company)

Contestants will compete for gold, silver and bronze, though the prizes have not yet been announced. The event is sponsored by streaming service Mubi, which, along with Bad Dog Theatre Company, is providing the prizes. The evening will end with a screening of the first episode of The Curse, the series Fielder co-created with Benny Safdie.

items: You can see You Can See Everything everywhere

blocks.text: Entry is free for both contestants and spectators, but the theatre's capacity is limited. People can sign up through the QR code on event posters or the RSVP link shared by the Instagram accounts of Mubi Canada and Bad Dog Theatre Company. An RSVP does not guarantee admission; organizers say entry will be first come, first served.
Organizers reported more than 100 people signed up as of Oct. 30.

The Toronto event follows a New York City contest held Oct. 25 in Washington Square Park, where Nathan Fielder lookalikes competed alongside Elizabeth Holmes impersonators. The contest was inspired by You Can See Everything, the hit documentary about Holmes co-directed by Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

Organized by comedian Maddy West and a friend, it drew dozens of people, with more than 200 responding to the event's registration form. Social media posts from the day showed contestants in Fielder-inspired outfits and Holmes's signature black turtlenecks and blonde hair. Joe Sivick won the Fielder category, and actor and comedian Nicole Travolta won the Holmes category.
The Nathan Fielder lookalike craze also crossed the Pacific, with a competition held in Sydney on Nov. 1.

A poster shared by X user Levi Fishman also advertises a Nathan Fielder lookalike contest at Lafayette Park in San Francisco on Nov. 7. The poster says: "Winner literally gets crowned the most Nathan of Fielder (crown and bragging rights)."
The format has a precedent beyond Fielder. A Timothée Chalamet lookalike contest in New York in 2024 drew a large crowd and made headlines when Chalamet himself briefly appeared.
Similar contests followed in other cities, including competitions for actors Paul Mescal in Dublin, and Jeremy Allen White in Chicago, and singer Harry Styles in London.

items: What's with all the celebrity lookalike contests?

blocks.text: The gatherings often start with a simple flyer or social post and turn into a public spectacle, with contestants dressing the part and spectators sharing photos and videos on social media. The Toronto contest is taking that familiar format indoors, with a deliberately Fielder-esque twist: rather than relying on resemblance alone, contestants will have to perform.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Christine Pagulayan is a Toronto-based producer and writer with CBC News, currently with the Entertainment unit. She has worked in various roles at CBC News Network and The National. She has also worked as a multiplatform reporter in Toronto, Winnipeg, Halifax and Moncton. You can reach her at christine.pagulayan@cbc.ca.
