articles.title: Ice hockey officials considering options after CAS order to reinstate Russia
articles.summary: Ice hockey's ruling body is deciding how to respond to a decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport that allows Russia back into international competition. Germany hasn't ruled out pulling out as…

image.caption: Russian players could soon again be seen at IIHF-sanctioned international ice hockey tournamentsImage: Kirill Kukhmar/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

blocks.text: The president of the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), Franz Reindl, announced shortly after the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) on Friday, that he had called a meeting of its main decision-making body for this Monday and Tuesday.

The Lausanne-based court had ruled that the IIHF must allow Russian national teams to take part in ice hockey world championships again. They had been barred from doing so since shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"Our task now is to implement this ruling responsibly," said Germany's Reindl, who was elected IIHF president just last month.

"Several championships are only weeks away, and changes to participation affect many people; players, teams, organizing committees and host cities. We will work closely with all of them to find practical solutions."

blocks.caption: Franz Reindl, 71, was elected president of the IIHF in early OctoberImage: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: The first tournament the CAS decision applies to is the World Juniors, to be held beginning on December 26 in Canada. Just how it will affect the tournament is not clear. Hockey Canada said it was in contact with the IIHF and had briefed Prime Minister Mark Carney's government on the decision.
Canada to 'maintain restrictions' on Russian athletes
Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand told public broadcaster CBC that she is "not comfortable" with allowing a Russian team to take part in the tournament in Alberta.

"This is a very unwelcome decision given the geopolitical situation, given the actions of Russia," she said. "All options are on the table, and I will say, again, I greet this decision with great disappointment."
Canada's secretary of state for sport, Adam van Koeverden, appeared to rule out Russian athletes being granted visas for the tournament

"Canada will maintain restrictions on the participation of Russian athletes at events hosted in Canada that receive funding from the Government of Canada and explore further options to ensure that the Russian government is held accountable," he said in a statement.
German hosts mull 'possible consequences for Worlds
Germany is also considering its options as it prepares to host the Men's Ice Hockey World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Düsseldorf and Mannheim next May.
"The German government takes a very critical view of the decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport, a government spokesman said on Sunday, according to the DPA news agency.
"The German government will discuss possible consequences of the ruling, including for the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship in Germany, with the German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) promptly."

blocks.caption: Frank Lutz is expected to meet with government officials in Berlin this weekImage: Adrian Goldberg/BEAUTIFUL SPORTS/picture alliance

blocks.text: The DEB's chief executive, Frank Lutz, is to travel to Berlin to discuss the matter with government officials this week. Speaking on broadcaster MagentaSport on the weekend, he conceded that surrendering Germany's hosting rights for the lucrative tournament was a possibility.

"I do not want to paint a black picture. I do not want to call the World Championship into question either. But of course, we at the DEB also have to consider the option of handing back this championship," he said.
Many disappointed, Russia delighted
Several other national ice hockey federations have expressed disappointment at the CAS decision, including those of Ukraine, Sweden, Finland, and Czechia.

The International Olympic Committee opened the door for Russian athletes to return to international competition when it lifted its ban of the Russian Olympic Committee in July. However, the IIHF had already decided to continue to exclude Russian teams for the 2026-27 season – over security concerns. The CAS decision – handed down after an appeal by Russia – found this reasoning was insufficiently proven.
Russian reaction to the ruling was, unsurprisingly, positive.

"Russia is returning to world hockey. This place rightfully belongs to us, and discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev told state television channel Vesti.

blocks.caption: The Russian Olympic Committee team won silver at their last tournament, the 2022 Winter Olympics in BeijingImage: Maxim Thore/Bildbyran/IMAGO

blocks.text: No return to business as usual
A boycott of the World Juniors, Men's World Championships or other tournaments by individual nations appears to be a possibility.

Latvia is prohibited by law from competing against Russian teams. Finland has said individual players would be free to opt-out of tournaments that include Russia, while Swedish Ice Hockey Association chairman Anders Larsson, who is a member of the IIHF Council, told Swedish news agency TT that "a boycott is not on the table."
However, at the same time he also noted that "our position is that Russia cannot participate in international championships in the current situation."
Further-reaching implications?
There has been the suggestion, that having won this victory at the CAS, Russia's next focus could be on football, where its national and club teams remain excluded from international competitions.
Russian FA general secretary Maxim Mitrofanov told state news agency Tass that there "should be one rule for all."

World football's governing body FIFA allowed a Russia boys' team to play under its national flag in the inaugural Under-15 World Cup and Festival in Azerbaijan, which kicked off last week and ends on Saturday.

articles.title: Wizz Air flight from London in emergency landing after bomb threat
articles.summary: A Hungarian fighter jet escorted the aircraft to Budapest after the threat was received mid-air.

blocks.text: A Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia has been escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat.
The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing at Budapest Liszt Ferenc International.
Authorities there "carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers", a spokesperson for Wizz Air said.

The airline later confirmed an inspection had been "completed and nothing was found", adding that the plane would depart again shortly. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendis confirmed his country provided the fighter jet to escort the flight.
According to flight tracking website FlightAware, Wizz Air flight 4302 departed Luton at 08:33 GMT and was due to arrive in the Bulgarian capital at 13:25 local time (11:25 GMT).
But the website said it landed in Budapest at 12:09 local time (11:09 GMT).
In a post on social media, Ruszin-Szendis said that after receiving the bomb threat, the Wizz Air flight had requested permission to land at the airport in Budapest.
"Within minutes, a Hungarian Defence Forces Gripen fighter jet took to the skies and provided an escort for the passenger aircraft", he said.
After this, the jet returned to its base and police took charge of the incident, he added.
The airline said that after the plane made the emergency landing, it taxied "to a designated stand" where the security checks were carried out.
Wizz Air added that it was "cooperating fully with the authorities", and that the safety of passengers and crew "remains our highest priority".

articles.title: European supermarkets targeted in second reported cyberattack
articles.summary: Supermarkets across Europe have been targeted in cyberattacks once again. Three weeks after a defrosting attack in France, supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported…

image.caption: Food had to be thrown out at a number of European supermarkets after freezers were remotely set to defrostImage: Fredrik Sandberg/TT NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden reported anomalies in their freezer systems on Monday in an apparent cyberattack similar to one in France three weeks ago in which unidentified malign actors were accused of having hijacked refrigeration systems — setting them to defrost and spoiling fresh and frozen foods.

In Monday's incident, Swedish supermarket chains ICA and Coop said "a limited number" of shops had been hit, with ICA spokeswoman Helena Johansson saying the company is "looking into what has happened and the scale of it."

"Fridges and freezers have either stopped working entirely or have been partially impaired," Coop spokesman Carlos Cancino told the French AFP news agency. He noted that six of roughly 800 Coop stores in Sweden had been impacted, adding, "I haven't received any information that this is a cyberattack."
Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize on Monday said an overnight "IT incident" had hit freezers in several of its stores in Belgium and Luxembourg.
In Ireland, public broadcasterer RTE reported that 13 supermarkets had been impacted.
Chains Carrefour, Intermarche and Spar were targeted as well, with Carrefour's Belgium spokesman Mich Vergauwen saying, "It's a cyberattack… There's no other reason."
Belgium's prosecutor's office opened a criminal investigation into the attack, the Reuters news agency quoted a spokesperson as saying.

European Commissioner ‌for Agriculture and ‌Food ​Christophe Hansen on Monday called the attacks "a deliberate attempt to disrupt Europe's food supplies," stating that ⁠while "food ​security is ​not currently ​at risk, ‌the food waste ​and ⁠impact on businesses ⁠are ​real."
"These incidents ‌show ​that cyberattacks can disrupt services, affect ​businesses and directly affect ⁠citizens’ ​daily lives" added ​a Commission ​spokesperson.

blocks.caption: Though no one has claimed responsibility, authorities are convinced that problems with freezer cooling and defrosting systems at European supermarkets are the result of remote cyberattacksImage: Marie Mannes/REUTERS

blocks.text: How are hackers getting into supermarket refrigeration systems?
As on October 12, Monday's disruption prompted the discarding of spoiled products and again raised concerns about food security.
The ICA Kvantum branch in Sjobo in southern Sweden said temperatures in their systems were remotely dialed up to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).

blocks.caption: Monday's outages in Sweden mirrored a similar situation in early October that saw dozens of supermarkets targeted in France Image: Fredrik Sandberg/TT NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sweden's National Cybersecurity Center boss John Billow told the Reuters news agency on Monday that his department is investigating.
"We have in recent weeks... identified that we have quite a lot of exposed ⁠operational technology devices in Sweden that ​we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch," he added.

That "exposed operational technology" includes everything from refrigerators and heating systems to security cameras, alarm networks and an expanding ‌range ​of devices that were once largely mechanical but are now often monitored and controlled remotely, creating new opportunities for cybercriminals as they seek to exploit security vulnerabilities.

articles.title: LA communities kick out Big Oil
articles.summary: After years of advocacy from residents and legal battles with Big Oil, LA has voted to ban drilling and phase out oil extraction in the city. It's the first city in the country to kick the oil…

image.caption: LA residents fought urban oil drilling for years — it's now been banned by LA City Image: Gissela C./STAND-L.A.

blocks.text: Los Angeles has become the largest city in the US to ban oil drilling, after years of lawsuits and campaigning by residents who raised the alarm over pollution and potential health risks from nearby wells.

"Frontline communities have pushed the city for a solution for this for over a decade," said local resident Wendy Miranda, who has campaigned for years with STAND-LA, a coalition of community groups working to end neighborhood oil drilling.

The ordinance, approved by the LA City Council on October 28, puts an immediate stop to oil extraction and bans re-drilling or deepening of wells, while existing operations must be phased out within city limits over the next 20 years.
Though LA City is only part of greater Los Angeles, the move affects hundreds of active wells and thousands of inactive ones, many located in working class communities of color.

"In South LA, working-class families have had corporations drilling across the street from their homes," said council president Marqueece Harris-Dawson in a statement. "No one should have to live near an oil drilling site."

blocks.caption: Oil infrastructure is running just a stone's throw away from homes in LA neighborhoodsImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: Rock Zierman, CEO of the California Independent Petroleum Association (CIPA), told DW, "CIPA believes this ordinance constitutes an unlawful taking of private property."
LA follows much smaller Culver City, also in California, in moving against urban oil production, and begins the process of ending its long, complex relationship with fossil fuels.
Why residents campaigned to end city oil drilling

California's oil industry expanded rapidly in the early 20th century, when the state produced roughly a quarter of the world's oil. Lots of that so-called black gold was around LA and as the city grew, homes, schools and businesses were built around existing oil infrastructure.

Today, wells can be found beneath residential areas, close to playgrounds, along the coast and in some of the city's most densely populated and largely working-class neighborhoods. Some have been permanently sealed or plugged for decades, while others remain active or are idle.
Under California law, an idle well is one that has not produced oil for two years. Unlike plugged wells, they can potentially return to production.
How LA is plugging hidden oil wells

Residents living near the active and inactive wells report strong odors, headaches, nausea and breathing difficulties. Another concern is air quality. Oil wells can release toxic pollutants, including benzene and hydrogen sulfide, and research has linked proximity to oil extraction with higher rates of respiratory illness and reduced lung function.

But both active and idle wells can also leak methane — a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change — while residents say occasional accidents or breakages send oil flowing down city streets.

"Frontline communities have been experiencing or have experienced for decades living near these toxic sites and having to pay for that with their health," said Miranda, a policy director with Esperanza Community Housing, a nonprofit providing affordable housing services.
Miranda told DW she and her mother both have asthma. The council vote "definitely represents hope," she added.
Previous attempts to ban oil production

LA City Council initially approved an ordinance to phase out oil extraction back in 2022 after successful lobbying by residents like Wendy Miranda. But oil companies challenged the measure in court, with industry groups successfully arguing that the city lacked the legal authority to impose the ban.
California subsequently passed legislation giving local governments greater power to regulate and restrict oil and gas operations, putting the possibility of a phaseout back on the table.

blocks.caption: Some oil wells are hidden in plain sight, such as this building hiding an active oil-drilling operationImage: Nils Hünerfürst/DW

blocks.text: In an emailed statement to DW, CIPA CEO Rock Zierman said energy companies were prepared to challenge the new ordinance.
Zierman added that it would make Angelenos more dependent on foreign oil from countries with lower environmental standards when they are "already struggling" with high gas prices.
"It sends the jobs, investment, and revenue elsewhere, while leaving Californians to pay the bill," said Zierman.

The relationship between local oil production and prices at the pump is not straightforward and is influenced by a number of factors, according to the California Energy Commission, the state's main energy policy agency. Those include the cost of crude oil, refining, transportation, distribution and local taxes.

Even though the US is the world's largest oil producer, it exports and imports crude oil, as well as refined petroleum products. Because oil is traded globally, US residents are exposed to the same price fluctuations as people elsewhere, no matter how much of the fossil fuel is produced domestically.

California's oil industry and the amount of oil it produces have been steadily declining since the 1980s. In the LA Basin, output is 43% lower than eight years ago, with the amount of oil extracted falling more rapidly than the number of open wells.
Who will foot the bill for the cleanup?

When wells stop producing, it is up to the oil operators to remove equipment and plug them. The state agency that regulates oil and gas, CalGEM, and the LA Fire Department oversee plugging operations, and also seal wells for which no-one takes responsibility.
But many have not yet been plugged — some 80% of idle wells in LA have been inactive for more than eight years, and about a third for over a century.

The cost of plugging a well also varies widely, with estimates ranging from hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. California law requires operators to submit plugging plans or face annual fines that increase with the amount of time the well has been idle.
But those fines aren't always paid. According to CalGEM's own data, the agency collected just $1 million out of $36 million in fines in 2025.

A report by Carbon Tracker also found that if all future profits from oil companies operating in California went to decommissioning wells, the state would still face a shortfall of $7 billion. The cost would by default fall to taxpayers, according to Carbon Tracker.

Miranda told DW that the next step for community activists is to reduce the 20-year timeline and have the oil sector "pay for this cleanup." For now, she is says both she and her mother are hopeful that future generations "can have better health and breathe cleaner air."

articles.title: Guardian Essential poll: record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup
articles.summary:
Growing disdain for gambling and animal cruelty concerns drive sliding interest in race that once ‘stopped the nation’

  • Get our

blocks.text: A record number of Australians are turning their backs on the Melbourne Cup, with more than two-thirds surveyed saying they have low or zero interest in the annual horse race.

Support for the Melbourne Cup has been sliding consistently for a number of years, but the Guardian Essential poll found just 9% of Australians said they had high interest in the race now – nearly half the proportion in 2025.
“The race that once stopped the nation is now just white noise for many,” Peter Lewis, chair of Essential Media, said.
The Guardian Essential poll of 1,003 Australians in late October highlights the latest erosion in popularity of the event amid growing ambivalence to the event.

Just 9% of people said they had high interest in the Cup, down 7 percentage points from 2025, with another 23% professing moderate interest, also down 3 points. About 29% of voters said they had low interest (up 5 points from last year), while another 39% said no interest at all (up 8 points).

The combined high and moderate interest came to only 32%, the lowest on record since Essential began asking this question in annual polling in November 2022. The combined low and no interest vote was 68%, jumping 12 points from last year to its highest on record.
In November 2022, the low and no interest vote came to a combined 52%; it was 62% in 2023, 52% in 2024, and 56% in 2025.
The “nup to the Cup” movement, backed by some high-profile politicians and celebrities, has contributed to declining support for the race.

But 62% of Australians nonetheless agreed the Melbourne Cup was a unique part of Australia’s national identity. That number remains a strong majority view, despite falling from 78% agreement when Essential asked this question in 2019.
Half of Australians (50%) believe the Cup promotes unhealthy gambling behaviour, up 3% since 2025, while 36% say they feel the Cup normalises animal cruelty, down 3 points from 2025.
Another 48% said they were less interested in the Cup than they used to be.
“The key driver appears to be a growing disdain for gambling, although concern for animal cruelty comes a close second,” Lewis said.
“More broadly this reflects the decline in unifying atonal moments in a world where more and more people have their experiences mediated by targeted advertising algorithms.”

Just 12% of voters in October’s poll said they regularly wagered on horse races and would bet on Tuesday’s Melbourne Cup, down 5 points from 2025. In contrast, 46% of people said they were not interested in the Cup and would not place a bet, up 6 points from last year.
Another 25% said they rarely bet on horses but would watch the race and place a bet, while 17% said they would watch but not bet.

articles.title: Reddit and libertarian group challenge Australia’s under-16s social media ban in high court
articles.summary:
Social network and Digital Freedom Project, led by NSW state MP John Ruddick, seek to overturn ban on grounds of implied freedom of political communication

Australia’s world-leading…

blocks.text: Australia’s world-leading under-16s social media ban will face its first major legal challenge on Tuesday, as Reddit and an advocacy group headed by a libertarian politician seek to overturn the law in the high court.

Nearly 11 months ago, 10 platforms – Snapchat, TikTok, YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Reddit, Kick, X, Twitch and Threads – were required to deactivate or suspend the accounts of users they determined to be aged under 16 years.
Since then, the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has said more than 5m accounts across the 10 services have been suspended as part of the ban.

Whether the ban will stay will be the subject of the high court hearings on Tuesday and Wednesday this week as Reddit and the Digital Freedom Project – led by New South Wales state Libertarian MP John Ruddick – seek to overturn the ban.

Australia does not have a guaranteed right to freedom of speech, and the case largely focuses on whether preventing under-16s from holding a social media account impermissibly burdens the implied freedom of political communication in Australian law.

Reddit has argued in its submission to the court that online platforms are a “common source of news and political information” in Australia. The company pointed to its “Ask Me Anything” sessions on the site where users have historically asked questions of politicians of candidates.

blocks.caption: NSW MP John Ruddick, leader of the Digital Freedom Project. Photograph: Mike Bowers/The Guardian

blocks.text: Teens, Reddit said, would not be able to make posts on politics, comment or react to political content, or engage with the social media accounts of the youth wings of the major political parties.

The Australian government has argued in its defence that the law serves the legitimate purposes of seeking to reduce the risk of harm for under-16s from social media platforms for the “harmful features” including algorithms, infinite scroll, persistent notifications and likes.

While the Digital Freedom Project adopted many of the same arguments on political communications burden as Reddit in its submission, the group is likely to face an additional hurdle with the government challenging the standing of the group to bring the case to the court.

Digital Freedom Group had initially had two teens – Noah Jones and Macey Nyland – as the original lead plaintiffs for the case as teens affected by the ban. However in July both were withdrawn from the case, leaving it to the advocacy group.
It is understood there was concerns that the teens would face potential legal costs against them in the event of a loss.

Digital Freedom Project has argued in its submission that some of its members are between the ages of 13 and 15, and the teens are likely to be presented as examples in the case, but the federal government has argued that as the plaintiff, Digital Freedom Project does not have standing to bring the case.
The federal government’s submission argues the group has not identified any activity of the group that is impeded by the ban.

Legal experts have been divided on the prospect of success. The constitutional law expert Prof Anne Twomey wrote last year that Reddit could be successful in highlighting the mismatch between the intended purpose of the law and the practical effect – if the restriction is not preventing children from the harms while also restricting their freedom of political communication.
after newsletter promotion

Luke Beck, professor of constitutional law at Monash University, wrote in the Guardian last year the cases were likely to fail, as the social media account ban only slightly reduces the overall volume of political communication in Australia, and 13-, 14- and 15-year-olds were not engaging in much political communication before the ban.
Beck said last week the extra hurdle for Digital Freedom Project to prove standing would also be difficult.

“The government is arguing that DFP is not impacted by the law so therefore can’t challenge it,” he said. “We’ll see what the high court says about advocacy groups having standing to challenge laws: traditionally the courts aren’t too keen.”

Many other countries are considering following Australia’s lead, but there have been concerns teens have been able to easily circumvent the ban. The federal opposition has also raised concerns that the number of accounts suspended may be inflated, while the government has refused to release numbers broken down by platform.

As the legal challengers get their day in court, the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, is also using new powers passed by parliament this year to investigate whether TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Instagram and Facebook are in compliance with the law, given the number of teens still holding accounts.
The companies could be facing the prospect of fines of up to nearly $100m a breach, if the regulator decides to take the case to the federal court.

The federal parliament is also debating the digital duty of care legislation mandating platforms take actions to prevent users experiencing harm on their platforms. Beck has said the passage of this legislation could present a pyrrhic victory for Reddit if it successfully overturns the ban.

The Australian government has made this argument in its submission in the case, stating the obligations of the digital duty of care bill would “require the same action” as the social media ban legislation.
“Namely, preventing children having accounts or providing children with accounts that do not have any of the [restricted] features.”

articles.title: NSW council refuses to show world-renowned Gaza artwork over ‘unacceptable’ safety risk
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Shoalhaven council says Wall of Tears installation by Phil Buehler posed risk to staff, visitors and tenants

  • Get our

blocks.text: A New South Wales local council has refused to show a world-renowned artwork about children killed in Gaza after asking organisers to investigate hiring “armed guards” to counter the risk of “community conflict” over the mural.

The group, Shoalhaven Friends of Palestine, was aiming to show the Wall of Tears installation by American artist Phil Buehler at the Shoalhaven Regional Gallery in Nowra on Tuesday, following the work being exhibited around Australia, including on the front lawns of Parliament House in Canberra in September.

The massive artwork pays homage to the 18,457 children killed in Gaza between 7 October 2023 and 19 July 2025 and was first shown in New York on 29 January to coincide with the second anniversary of the death of Hind Rajab, a five-year-old left to bleed out among the bodies of six family members after their car was targeted by an Israeli tank.

Shoalhaven city council asked the group to “investigate” the use of “armed guards” in a risk assessment seen by Guardian Australia. The perceived risks included “protest, counter-protest, community conflict,” and “verbal abuse, intimidation or disruption arising from politically sensitive subject matter”.
The group was also asked to reduce the exhibition window from eight days to three days and restrict attendance to RSVPs only in the gallery, which would have “locked doors”.
Organisers were also requested to no longer advertise the event due to potential “reputational risk” for the gallery or council due to their decision to host the exhibition.
“We were like, ‘You’ve got to be kidding me,’ but we still wrote back to them and said we would meet all the requirements you want,” said Annette Pham, a member of the group.
“We didn’t even know where we could get armed guards, or if you could get them.”
Despite this, email correspondence shows Andrew Constance – the chief executive of the council and former Liberal MP – decided against hosting the event, citing staff safety concerns.

Pham wrote to the council stating she was “deeply disappointed” by the decision and said the “very suggestion that armed guards might be necessary for an exhibition commemorating dead children is deeply disturbing”.

“We are organising a memorial art exhibition, not an event for which Council has disclosed any specific credible threat of violence requiring consideration of armed protection and metal screening,” Pham wrote in her email.

blocks.caption: The Wall of Tears mural on display in New York City in January. Photograph: Phil Buehler

blocks.text: A council spokesperson said in a statement that they had considered the request, but “the installation was deemed to present an unacceptable level of risk to gallery staff, visitors and tenants of the building”.
The council did not respond directly to a question from Guardian Australia about what had triggered the safety concerns.
Pham has now arranged for the work to be installed at Berry Uniting Church on Thursday.
after newsletter promotion
‘They’re children’
Buehler said he was shocked his artwork, which has been shown in cities around the world, could be perceived as posing a safety risk.
“They’re children. They’re like your children, my children,” he said, adding it refers to death toll figures accepted by Israel. The artwork draws from Guardian reporting.

“If you look at the pictures on that mural … There’s kids in their little graduation outfits holding diplomas, they’re holding soccer balls. They’re there with their siblings, or on their father’s shoulder. It was the hardest artwork I’ve ever made, to just live with [what happened to these children], for the time it took to make it.”
“If people would just look at that, how can that be dangerous? The danger is put on by other people who are trying to turn it into something it’s not.”
The artwork has been touring around Australia, including in Adelaide where it was first shown, and Perth where it was shown at the Western Australian state parliament.
Dr Mairead Heaney is part of Perth Doctors Medical Aid for Palestine which helped arrange the exhibition at the WA parliament and the federal Parliament House in Canberra.
She said a number of Labor, Greens and independent MPs visited the artwork when it was displayed in Canberra, including Labor MP Tony Zappia, who made a statement to parliament about it.
Zappia said in his speech: “The banner is a sad reminder of the level of Palestinian human losses, suffering, and daily violations they endure, while much of the world looks away.”

articles.title: A Paralympian vs a former TV news anchor - and other US Senate races to watch
articles.summary: All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber. Here's a quick guide.

blocks.text: Opponents in Iowa - Democrat Josh Turek and Republican Ashley Hinson

Millions of Americans are about to decide the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.
All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.
A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.
Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.
There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report, external.
Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.
In a nutshell:

This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Dan Sullivan is aiming for his third term against Alaska Native Mary Peltola

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Dan Sullivan is aiming for his third term against Alaska Native Mary Peltola
Story of the race:
The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.

Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner.

Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race.
The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge.
Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.
How they got here:

Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.

One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the survivors of US politics.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Susan Collins, the incumbent, takes on logger Troy Jackson in Maine

blocks.text: Susan Collins, the incumbent, takes on logger Troy Jackson in Maine
Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections.
Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump.
Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election.

But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate.

Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).

Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.

James Talarico aims to end a decades-long electoral drought for the Democrats in Texas - and show that one of the Republicans' main strongholds could be in play for the 2028 presidential election. His match-up with Ken Paxton has become the most expensive Senate race ever.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump ally Ken Paxton (L) faces a challenge from former teacher James Talarico (R) in the Texas contest

blocks.text: Trump ally Ken Paxton (L) faces a challenge from former teacher James Talarico (R) in the Texas contest
Republican Paxton knows his party has been winning statewide races in Texas for more than 30 years.
Texas State Representative James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminary student, is the latest Democrat hoping to break his party's long losing streak.

Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. It is a challenging national political environment for conservatives and there are several state issues like data centre construction and aggressive immigration enforcement that have cut against their party. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.

The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".

Supported by more than $170m in funds from tech mogul Elon Musk, Paxton has attempted to paint Talarico as a liberal who is out of touch with Texans on issues like transgender rights, law enforcement, immigration and energy policy.

A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.
Before he entered public service, Paxton spent 14 years launching and building his own law firm. He served in the state House and Senate before becoming the chief legal officer in Texas.
Talarico taught at a middle school in San Antonio, in a neighbourhood he has described as one of the poorest in the state. He has studied theology and names Pope Leo as a "spiritual hero".

This is one of the most bitter contests, with left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed aiming to keep this crucial seat in Democratic hands. He is up against Mike Rogers, a Republican former FBI agent who received a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's defeated Democratic rival, only adding to the acrimony that has characterised this race from the start.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Former public health official El-Sayed (L) will contest Michigan with former congressman Rogers (R)

blocks.text: Former public health official El-Sayed (L) will contest Michigan with former congressman Rogers (R)
A doctor and public health official, El-Sayed is one of the most left-wing Senate nominees this election cycle.
He supports a government-run health insurance system and the abolition of ICE. His strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension in the party.
Rogers, who emphasises his military and intelligence background, has managed to maintain Trump's support despite decrying his Canada tariffs and his Russia diesel deal.
He has also diverged from the president by calling for a quick end to the war with Iran. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate.
As well as attacking him for his politics, Trump and Rogers have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood; El-Sayed has denounced the organisation.
The president has also invoked 9/11 and even called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in Michigan before his medical studies in the US and UK and subsequent work in the sector. Rogers, 63, served in the US Army and in the FBI before entering Congress and emerging as a key advocate of US surveillance policies.

Trump made the trip to Iowa on his final day of campaign rallies, such is its importance. Polls have it as a toss-up between Republican and former TV news host Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, who won gold at basketball at two Paralympic Games.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ashley Hinson, who was once a local news reporter, is up against ex-basketballer Josh Turek in Iowa

blocks.text: Ashley Hinson, who was once a local news reporter, is up against ex-basketballer Josh Turek in Iowa
Farms, tariffs and Trump have all emerged as key issues in the closely-watched race.

Hinson has slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.

Meanwhile, Turek argues that Trump's tariffs have led to "farmageddon" in the largely rural state. He has also sought to convince voters that the war in Iran has led to rising fuel and fertiliser costs.
Hinson has cast Turek as a candidate who would vote as an "East Coast liberal".
The two have also clashed on issues ranging from taxes and social security to immigration. The last time a Democrat won a federal election in Iowa was nearly 20 years ago.

Hinson, 43, is a former local news reporter who says her journalistic background helps her understand the issues faced by the state's farmers and small businesses. Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida, going through multiple surgeries before representing the USA at wheelchair basketball at four Paralympic Games, twice triumphantly.

A Democratic victory in Kansas would upend 94 years of history - the last time this Midwestern state elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Senator Roger Marshall is the Republican trying to avoid a humbling defeat, while first-time candidate and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton is the Democrat trying to break records.

blocks.caption: Image caption, In Kansas, both the incumbent Roger Marshall (L) and the challenger Adam Hamilton (R) highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans

blocks.text: In Kansas, both the incumbent Roger Marshall (L) and the challenger Adam Hamilton (R) highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans
Marshall has closely aligned himself as a Trump-aligned, pro-farmer candidate.

Hamilton, who once considered running as an independent, has pitched himself as a candidate that can bridge the partisan divide. He has largely campaigned on a message of lower costs and protecting healthcare access.
Marshall has sought to attack Hamilton's record as a pastor, describing him as "too woke" for the conservative state.

Marshall, meanwhile, has been under scrutiny ever since reports emerged that he sued patients unable to pay their medical bills. He told Fox News the story was a hit job by the left media and senior Democrats.
The tight race is broadly seen as a potentially ominous sign for Republicans.
A Hamilton victory would be seen as a sign of increasing dissatisfaction with Trump's policies - particularly on economics - in territory that was once considered safe for the party.

Both Marshall, 66, and Hamilton, 62, highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans who are in close touch with local issues. Marshall worked for 25 years as an obstetrician, delivering some 5,000 babies, while his rival Hamilton founded a church which became the centre of the largest United Methodist congregation in America.

Trump won this state with ease in 2024 and no-one a year ago considered it in play for the midterms. But Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown who is running to get his old job back, having represented Ohio in the Senate for many years before losing his seat.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Ohio race sees Jon Husted (L), who replaced JD Vance, compete against Sherrod Brown (R), who is aiming for a comeback

blocks.text: The Ohio race sees Jon Husted (L), who replaced JD Vance, compete against Sherrod Brown (R), who is aiming for a comeback
Husted was appointed in 2025 to the Senate seat vacated by Vice-President JD Vance, and is now running to serve the rest of Vance's term.
He promises to use his business experience to bring jobs and growth to Ohio.
In a different election cycle he would probably be the favourite to win this onetime swing state that has become reliably red in the Trump era.
But Husted is facing a formidable challenge from Brown, who has high name recognition from three decades representing Ohio in Congress.
Brown is known as a champion of workers and was advocating economic populist policies long before others in his party.
The race is a referendum on Trump's economic policies, in particular his trade wars that have impacted the manufacturing and auto industries that underpin Ohio's economy.

Husted, 59, began life in a foster home and was in the world of business before politics; he was an elite American football player at college and his physique has been repeatedly praised by President Trump at rallies. Brown, 73, was introduced to political activism from a young age and was recruited into local politics even before graduating from Yale.
By Bernd Debusmann, Daniel Bush and Anthony Zurcher in Washington, and James FitzGerald and Tom Geoghegan in London.

articles.title: ICC wraps up pre-trial hearings as Duterte’s November 30 case nears
articles.summary: Duterte skips his last status conference after waiving his right to appear. He will, howver, have to personally appear every day once his trial starts on November 30.

items: The ICC Trial Chamber III concluded its status conference ahead of former President Rodrigo Duterte's trial for crimes against humanity, scheduled to start on November 30.

Duterte waived his right to attend the last status conference, but will be expected to attend daily during the trial, which will include opening statements from the prosecution and victim representatives.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III wrapped up its status conference hearings on Monday, November 2, weeks before the start of former president Rodrigo Duterte’s trial for his crimes against humanity case.

A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial. This is to ensure that the schedule and other legal matters proceed smoothly during the actual trial days.
Duterte skipped his last status conference after waiving his right to appear. The chamber granted his request.

“Mr. [Peter] Haynes, we’ve agreed exceptionally because this is not likely to be a particularly lengthy status conference that Mr. Duterte need not attend this morning. But once the actual trial starts, we will expect, as we said, [his] attendance on a daily basis,” said Presiding Judge Joanna Korner.

The former president, who has been detained at The Hague, Netherlands since March 2025, appeared during his status conferences on September 16 and October 13, respectively. The September 16 schedule marked Duterte’s first-ever ICC appearance since his arrest in 2025.

blocks.caption: Rodrigo Duterte attends ICC hearing in person for the first time

blocks.text: During the Monday hearing, the parties said they will have opening statements when the trial starts on November 30. The prosecution will deliver a statement, followed by the Common Legal Representatives of the Victims or the lawyers of the victims.
Traditionally, the defense cannot deliver an opening statement, but Korner said the defense might want to give at least an outline of what Duterte’s defense will be.

“And I want to know if you’ve considered applying, not to open in full, but to give, if you like, the public and the court an outline of what your defense is going to be, along the lines of what happens in other jurisdictions?” Korner asked.

“We will certainly finalize that position within the next few days, and we’ll let you know for scheduling purposes. But I think it’s more likely than not that I will say something at the start of the case, given its stature, really, and the character of the accused and his status,” said Haynes, Duterte’s defense lawyer.
The prosecution said they will open their case and take about four to six hours, and around three hours for the victims.
Principal Counsel Office of Public Counsel for Victims Paolina Massidda said they asked the chamber if they can use Tagalog (Filipino) for parts of their opening statement.
“Our request is more, during the opening statement, we will make some remark in quoting parts of a narrative that victims provided to us, and we’d like to do that in Tagalog,” said Massidda.

“And the purpose is a lot of victims will be connecting to the hearing. For them, it’s also important to listen how we convey to the chamber what they narrated to us and their experiences, and they relate and connect much more if that is done in Tagalog,” she added.

But Korner reiterated that the Rome Statute or the treaty that created the ICC, provides for only English and French as the court’s working languages. Apart from saying that there are interpreters, Korner said Tagalog is not the language of all the victims.

“So while we understand that you want to relate to the victims, you want the victims to relate to what’s being said, all of it, everything you say, as I understand it…. will be translated in any event, interpreted,” the presiding judge explained.

blocks.caption: ICC wraps up pre-trial hearings as Duterte’s November 30 case nears

blocks.text: For the first batch of evidence, Korner said the chamber will adopt a new schedule. Like what had been announced in the past, there will be 30-minute breaks per hour to heed the experts’ advice that no sitting for Duterte beyond one hour. The schedule of sessions is as follows:

items: 12:30 to 1:30 pm (lunch break)

blocks.text: For the hearings in 2027, the parties — prosecution, victims, and defense — proposed the following schedule:

items: January 11 to 29 (three weeks)
One-week break (Feb 1-5)
February 8 to 19 (two weeks)
Two-week break (Feb 22-March 5)
March 8 to 26 (final three weeks)

blocks.text: “I think, from all of us, if it’s possible to have the week of the 22nd of February off, and that is because that is when it’s a school break for all the different schools, the Dutch, British, French, and so that affects many people, I think, on the different teams,” said the Prosecution’s senior trial lawyer Julian Nicholls.

Meanwhile, the chamber said the prosecution will present five witnesses for the first batch of evidence. The first witness will take six hours, a “little much shorter” time for the other two, then four hours each for the last two witnesses.

Korner also asked the prosecution if it was possible to prioritize the in-person witnesses, before presenting witnesses who will testify via video link. Nicholls said they have at least 29 witnesses who will testify online.
Once again, the large data set of evidence against Duterte, a subject of debate in the last status conferences, was brought up.
Nicholls said they will discuss the matter to straighten things out.

“And so we’re planning on having meetings this week to see about ways we may be able to reach agreements, which, as we started talking about this, if we can come to some agreements, that may sort of extract the relevance of a lot of, or not relevance, but extract the need to rely on much of that if we can come to some agreements,” said the prosecution lawyer.

The court also went into private or closed sessions multiple times during the Monday hearing. The chamber does this when there are matters that are private or confidential in nature that need to be discussed. – Rappler.com

articles.title: P459B worth of DPWH projects awarded to dubious contractors --COA
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged 11,391 Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) projects worth P459 billion, which were awarded to contractors with questionable financial capacity.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 9:31pm
The Commission on Audit (COA) has flagged 11,391 Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) projects worth P459 billion, which were awarded to contractors with questionable financial capacity.

"Review of the 27,094 sampled infrastructure contracts disclosed that 11,391 contracts with an aggregate contract cost of P459.262 billion involved bidders whose submitted Statements of Ongoing Government and Private Contracts did not completely reflect their ongoing and awarded but not yet stated contractual commitments," according to a COA Audit Report quoted on a "24 Oras" report by Maki Pulido.

"The incomplete declaration of ongoing contractual commitments resulted in Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) computations that did not fully consider the bidders’ outstanding obligations, thereby overstating their available contracting capacity and affecting the reliability of financial eligibility assessments during the post-disqualification," the COA report added.
The report said that 198 contractors should not have been given additional contracts because their previous contracts have not been completed.

"Audit disclosed that 198 contractors awarded to certain contractors in DPWH North Manila DEO in NCR initially met the NFCC requirements during the preliminary examination of bids. However, the same contractors were subsequently awarded multiple contracts under the Early Procurement Activities," COA said.

"When these contracts were considered collectively, the contractors’ remaining NFCC was no longer sufficient to cover the cumulative ABCs, indicating that their available contracting capacity had been exhausted," it added.

The incomplete declaration of ongoing contractual commitments resulted in Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) computations that did not fully consider the bidders’ outstanding obligations, thereby overstating their available contracting capacity and affecting the reliability of financial eligibility assessments during the post disqualification.
One of the contractors was awarded four more contracts worth P530 million, even though it should have been eligible to take on only P81 million worth of projects.
Another contractor secured seven contracts worth P1 billion, despite being eligible to take on only P189 million worth of projects.
According to the COA report, the following regions recorded the highest number of contracts awarded to bidders with incomplete documentary requirements:

items: Region I – 1,893 contracts worth P45.76 billion
Region X – 1,328 contracts worth P63.55 billion
Region IV-A – 1,289 contracts worth P41.65 billion
Region II – 1,213 contracts worth P43.55 billion
Region III – 1,134 contracts worth P40.28 billion

blocks.text: MIMAROPA (Region IV-B) had the highest total value of contracts awarded to bidders with incomplete documents, at P65.70 billion across 419 contracts.

The DPWH said it validated the contractors' Net Financial Contracting Capacity (NFCC) during the post-qualification stage. It explained that the projects had not yet been awarded when the contractors submitted their bids, so these were not included in the NFCC computation.
The COA, however, said the DPWH may review bidders' qualifications at any stage of the procurement process.
The DPWH also had information that the contractors had already secured other projects, which could serve as grounds for reassessing their capacity to take on additional contracts.

“The findings of the COA in their Audit Observation Memoranda covering prior years are forwarded to the concerned Implementing Office so they can address the same. We shall coordinate with the IOs on the status of their compliance and will share an update once we have their responses,” said DPWH Secretary Giovanni Lopez.
GMA News has sought comment from former DPWH chiefs Manuel Bonoan and Vince Dizon, but has yet to receive a response. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany's chancellor called for Korean unity. Does Seoul want that?
articles.summary: Germany, like Korea, was once divided by rival political systems and by one of the world's most fortified borders. Chancellor Merz called for a reunified Korea during his recent visit — but the…

image.caption: The South Korea government officially still pursues reunification, but the younger generations' attitudes have shiftedImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The story of South and North Korea — two nations that share history, language and much of their cultural heritage — sounds familiar to Germans.
Their own country spent decades divided by opposing regimes until geopolitical winds shifted and allowed East and West Germany to reunite peacefully in 1991.

Just two years later, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl visited the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on the Korean Peninsula and expressed hope that South and North Korea would also be reunited by the end of the decade.

That never materialized. Some 35 years since Germany achieved its dream of reunification, Seoul and Pyongyang are still bitterly divided by political systems, economy, and their geopolitical alliances.
German chancellor and president tour Asia
Overlooking the DMZ, which separates the two Koreas, on Friday Chancellor Friedrich Merz could only repeat the hopes stated by Kohl in 1993.

"We Germans know how painful the division of a country is," Merz stated in a message shared on social media. "We also know that whoever stands firm in their values and has the courage for dialogue can tear down walls."
"We wish the people in Korea unity in freedom," Merz said.
To analysts following the day-to-day inter-Korean politics, this sounds like a distant dream.
Young Koreans ask 'why bother' with reunification
As the Koreas continue to eye each other warily across the DMZ, their dramatic differences in wealth and political freedom are clearly on display.
But the biggest single issue might be that neither side appears to want reunification.

"The feeling has changed in the last couple of decades," Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at Kyung Hee University, told DW. "Younger South Koreans just see the North as another country that happens to be next to us, is poor and threatening, and they have no sentimental attachment to it, like older generations do."
"More and more people are asking why they should bother about reunification," he said.
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

A study by Seoul National University's Institute for Peace and Unification Studies in September indicated that 39.1% of South Koreans believed reunification was impossible, the highest proportion since the survey was started some two decades ago.

Many were concerned about the vast amounts of money that it would take to build the North's infrastructure, including roads, hospitals, schools and all other requirements for a modern functioning society.

Officially, South Korea's government has not abandoned reunification as a national objective. Its constitution still calls for peaceful union based on freedom and democracy, but Choo points out recent governments are promoting the idea far less frequently than in the past.
North Korea's clear signal against unity
North Korea has not been nearly so reticent about where it stands on the matter.

"In December 2023, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced that the constitution was being changed and that peaceful reunification was no longer possible," Choo said. "Instead, South Korea would be seen as a hostile rival and that he no longer had any intention of bringing the two together."
The revised North Korean constitution was approved in March 2026 and Kim's regime has moved aggressively to scrub all references to reconciliation and national unity.

"I do not think the North can make it any clearer that it has no intention of getting any closer to South Korea," said Mason Richey, a professor of politics and international relations at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul. He added that analysts, officials and ordinary Koreans in the South "roll their eyes" when the issue of Korean reunification crops up.
Beyond the lack of desire on both sides, there are a number of additional challenges that would need to be overcome, he said.
North Korea's regime wishes to protect its own power and prestige, which would inevitably be under threat if a democratic system were introduced for a unified nation.

Bridging the enormous gap in economic development would be a huge undertaking that would put immense pressure on the South, Richey said, even if outside assistance were forthcoming. And while a united Germany has been able to bring its regions to relatively comparable levels, it is worth noting that East Germany in 1990 was still substantially more developed than North Korea is today.
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
United Korea would pose major issues for US and China

Nominal GDP in North Korea is $31.7 billion a year. In the South, it is $1.85 trillion a year, or 58 times bigger, according to Bank of Korea statistics for 2024. With North Korea having roughly one-half population size of the South, the GDP per capita in the North is just $1,230 (€1,097) against nearly $36,000 in the South.

Professor Choo said reunification would not just be a domestic issue. The two nations have divided strategic and security loyalties, with the South allied to the US and the North tied to China and increasingly, Russia.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine

"Those superpowers would not want to give up their ally for reunification as it would be a major strategic issue for them, as well," Choo said. "The US would not want a united Korea that leaned towards China, and Beijing would resist reunification if it meant the US could have its military on the Chinese border in what is presently North Korea. That's just impossible for either side to imagine."

Ultimately, he said, the present status quo on the peninsula may be an imperfect solution, but it is the best way of preserving regional stability. A decade into the future, however, the economic, social and security situations may have radically altered — "and that is why we can never say never."

articles.title: Global pedestrian Karl Bushby returns home to UK after 28-year trek
articles.summary: Karl Bushby, a British man who traveled 50,000 km without transport over the past 28 years, has come home. Starting in Chile, he crossed the Americas, Russia and parts of Central Asia and Europe —…

image.caption: Karl Bushby has returned home after 28 yearsImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived back his hometown in England on Monday after crossing four continents on foot.
He was met by a cheering crowd of some 500 people in the northeastern city of Hull at the end of his 50,000 km (31,000 mile) journey, which began in the far south of South America in 1998.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team, Earth. That's what it took to get me back," Bushby told the crowd.
On his trip, he obeyed two rules: to avoid all forms of motorized transport to advance; and not to return until he had finished what he had set out to do.
A very final leg of his journey was to take him to north Hull, where he was to reunite with his mother, Angela, his 36-year-old son, Adam, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

blocks.caption: Bushby was welcomed by a large crowd in his hometown of HullImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Bushby experience on his epic journey?
Bushby, a former paratrooper, began his adventure in Chile aged 29 after a marriage breakup that saw his wife return to Northern Ireland with their son.

During the trip, he crossed an iced-over Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer in 2006 — nearly losing his life in the process — and, returning to Britain early last month, he swam the English Channel from northern France to Dover over four days.

He interrupted, or was forced to pause, his journey several times, including when he was refused a visa by Russia, which caused a journey originally planned to take 12 years to last more than double that time.
He also spent some jail time in Panama for entering the country without a visa.
The COVID-19 pandemic also caused delays, and he spent some time living at a base in Mexico.
But he always resumed the trek at the exact spot where he had left off.

blocks.caption: Bushby transported the necessaries largely on a handcartImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: The famous German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled "Walk of Life."
In an interview with the AFP news agency from northern France in September, Bushby expressed apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
"I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again," he said.

articles.title: ICC adopts 1-hour trial blocks with 30-minute breaks for Duterte trial
articles.summary: The ICC Trial Chamber III has adopted a trial schedule of one-hour blocks separated by 30-minute breaks for the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 8:30pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has adopted a trial schedule of one-hour blocks separated by 30-minute breaks for the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, acting on expert advice.
Trial Chamber III adopted the modified sitting schedule during the fifth and final status conference for the case, held at the ICC in The Hague on Monday.
Duterte was not present after the court granted a defense request excusing him from the proceeding.
“In order to accommodate what the experts advised in respect to Mr. Duterte, we'll run now from 10 [a.m.] to 11 [a.m.], 11:30 [a.m.] to 12:30 [p.m.],” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.

“There will be a one-hour break for lunch… But I think this is necessary because of the circumstances of the case to keep those breaks and also finish at a time which allows everybody to deal with matters outside the trial,” she added.
In a decision made public on October 8, Trial Chamber III found Duterte fit to stand trial and instructed the ICC Registry to make necessary arrangements for the court proceedings.
Among the measures recommended by the Registry was a sitting schedule organized into one-hour blocks.
Under the adopted schedule, Duterte’s trial proceedings are expected to run from 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., resume from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and break for lunch from 12:30 p.m. to 1:30 p.m.
Trial proceedings will resume from 1:30 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. and will continue following the same pattern of one-hour sessions separated by 30-minute breaks.
The trial proper in the case against Duterte is set to open on November 30, 2026. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades
articles.summary: Ugandan troops first deployed to Somalia in 2007 as part of an international military coalition to battle Islamic insurgents. But the mission has faced mounting pressure since a US decision to…

image.caption: Ugandan forces have been supporting Somali troops fighting militants for almost 20 yearsImage: Farah Abdi Warsameh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Uganda announced on Monday that it had begun pulling its troops out of Somalia, where it has been a key player in efforts to counter insurgents for almost two decades.
"The first cohort of troops under the phased withdrawal operation have already arrived back in Uganda," a statement from the Ugandan military said.
Uganda was the first country to send troops to Somalia as part of an African Union peacekeeping force set up in 2007 to support the Somali government battling Al-Shabab Islamist militants.

Uganda "will gradually withdraw all its forces in Somalia, including those currently deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) by the close of 2027," the military's statement added, referring to the latest African Union mission.
Around 4,500 Ugandan troops are stationed in Somalia as part of AUSSOM, as well as about 2,000 deployed under bilateral agreements.

The Ugandan army said its withdrawal "will mark the end of Uganda's enduring 20-year peace and stabilization support operations in Somalia, permitting the Somali Armed Forces to assume full responsibility for security in the country."
Jihadist groups in Africa and their links
An initial contingent of 109 Ugandan soldiers left the Somali capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, local media reported.
Why is Uganda withdrawing its troops from Somalia?
The future of the African Union mission, AUSSOM, has been thrown into doubt following a recent US decision to end funding for a UN logistics office the military coalition relies on.

Washington, the coalition's biggest donor, has voiced frustration with a lack of progress in the fight against Al-Shabab, which continues to control large swaths of central Somalia. The US has also accused the Somali government of failing to unite the country and implement political reforms.
Somali civilians caught in crossfire as US strikes militants
Uganda's withdrawal announcement on Monday also came as the UN ended its political mission in Somalia.

The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia closed on Saturday after more than three decades of peacebuilding in the East African country, transferring responsibility to the Somali government and various UN agencies.
Somalia is due to hold elections in May next year, but insecurity and opposition disputes are threatening to derail the process.

Somalia has been gripped by a deadly insurgency led by Al-Shabab for more than two decades. While Ugandan forces have played a crucial role in driving the militants from the capital and several major towns, the group has recaptured territory in recent years and now controls significant areas in the center and south of the country.
