articles.title: How Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria
articles.summary: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the…

image.caption: Iliana Yotova (center) addresses the press after winning the Bulgarian presidential election runoff on Sunday, garnering 57.6% of the voteImage: BGNES

blocks.text: "We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.
With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.
Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.
But is it really as simple as all that?
First-round surprise

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.
Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

blocks.caption: Yotova, who succeeded Ruman Radev as president when he stepped down to run for prime minister earlier this year, is the first woman to be elected president of BulgariaImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.
While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.
Decisive victory, clear divide
While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.
This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.
'President of peace'
This divide was also evident during the campaign.

blocks.caption: Candidates Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) faced each other in Sunday's presidential election runoffImage: Desislava Kulelieva/BNT

blocks.text: While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.
At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.
Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."
"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.
Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue
In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.
Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.
The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea
In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria's former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-UkrainianImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."
Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.
How other voters voted

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.
To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.
Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.
Bulgaria in the EU and NATO

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.
According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

articles.title: Canadian among the dead in Spanish high-speed rail crash
articles.summary: A Canadian was among those killed last week in a high-speed train collision in Toledo, Global Affairs Canada has confirmed.

image.caption: People are shown at a funeral mass on Saturday for the 69 fatal victims of a high-speed train collision last week in Toledo, Spain. (Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·Updated
A Canadian was among those killed last week in a high-speed train collision in Toledo, Global Affairs Canada has confirmed.
Citizens from several countries died in crash, along with 54 Spaniards
"At this time, Global Affairs Canada is aware of the death of a Canadian citizen in the train crash in Spain," it said in a statement Monday. Another six Canadians were hurt in the crash Oct. 28.

"Our thoughts are with their families and loved ones as well as all of those affected," GAC said, adding that it is providing consular assistance and working with local authorities to gather more information.
In all, 526 passengers and 12 crew members were affected by last week's crash between the two trains, which happened near the town of Urda in central Spain.

The Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla La Mancha issued a statement Sunday, providing more information about the 69 people who died, after the victims were identified by the country's Center for Integrated Data.
Also among the dead were 54 people from Spain, along with citizens from France, the United States, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia, Portugal and the Czech Republic, Spanish officials have said.

It was the second major fatal accident this year involving the same rail companies on the same line after a January crash killed 46, reopening a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain's high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe.
Did human error cause Spain's deadly high-speed train crash? | About That

The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of the automatic-signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorized to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
Puente has thus far resisted calls from opposition parties to resign.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site late last week and has pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy.
The crash occurs as Sánchez and his Socialists are campaigning to stay in power, ahead of a Nov. 29 election.

The Spanish government was already facing discontent over housing costs and high rents, along with corruption allegations and criticism from right-wing parties of its liberal migration policies compared to other European countries.
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: Filipino embalmers – last caretakers of the dead, seldom cared for
articles.summary: Part 2: Trainers say a decade of reforms professionalized the embalming industry, but regulation, data, and pay have not kept pace

blocks.text: PART 1 | Inside the world of Filipino embalmersLast of 2 parts
When Jonnel Cribello received his license to embalm in 2009, one question followed him everywhere.
“The most frequent question people asked me [was] whether I washed my hands before shaking theirs,” he said.

A registered nurse who once dreamed of becoming a surgeon, Cribello turned to embalming after coming across a media feature on an embalming school. “If I wanted to work with the human body, the easiest route for me then was to work in the mortuary industry,” he said.

Today, he helps teach the next generation of embalmers as an accredited trainer and program director at the Philippine College of Advanced Studies (PCAS) in Cebu, one of only four active accredited embalming schools in the country and the only one outside Luzon.
Embalmers disinfect, preserve, and restore a body so families can hold a wake — often for days — before burial or cremation.
But while the industry has made strides in shedding its perception as dirty work, the systems around it — licensing, data, and pay — have been slower to catch up with other medical-adjacent fields.
For years, embalmers were seen as untidy and uneducated, said James Patrick Ovejera, president of the Professional Embalmers Association of the Philippines Inc. (PEAP).

“There was an idea that it’s dirty work, the person is untidy, the person is illiterate, and the person is technically a low-class person,” he said. “There were even depictions in the movies wherein it’s a person that works in a dark place… a hunchback.”
That image began to shift around 2010, when the Department of Health (DOH) set out to professionalize the field, Ovejera said.

The rules governing embalming date back to 1975, when then-president Ferdinand E. Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 856, or the Code on Sanitation of the Philippines. Its chapter XXI, on the disposal of dead persons, covers everything from burial grounds to funeral and embalming establishments.

Detailed rules for embalmers came only in 1996, more than two decades later. They called for the DOH to create a Committee of Examiners for Undertakers and Embalmers (DOH-CEUE), which licenses embalmers and accredits training schools.

In 2010, the DOH reinstated the committee with new members, who worked with the University of the Philippines to streamline the curriculum and licensure exam, under Administrative Order No. 2010-0033. The order also, for the first time, mandated minimum wage for all embalmers.

The committee and the five training schools at the time then went region by region to explain the rules to local officials. Feedback led to new measures, including a refresher program for embalmers with long-expired licenses and a Filipino version of the exam, which was previously in English.

“There are a lot of people [who] are very skilled coming from the provinces…but they couldn’t really understand English well,” said Ovejera. At the time, he had been teaching at the Philippine Embalmers and Undertakers Review and Training Center (PEURTC), and enlisted in the roadshow efforts.
In 2018, embalmers like Ovejera formed PEAP as their own professional counterpart to the Philippine Mortuary Association, which represents funeral homeowners.
“At the time, there was no collective body representing us, and we wanted to do something about that,” he said.

blocks.caption: LEARNING. Embalming students at PCAS watch an instructor lead a demonstration on a cadaver. Photo courtesy of PCAS

blocks.text: Under current DOH rules, aspiring embalmers need a high school diploma, at least 140 hours of instruction from an accredited institution, and proof that they have embalmed at least 10 cadavers within a year. They then take a licensure exam held twice a year, every March and September.

Under rules revised in 2021, licenses are issued by the DOH’s Health Facilities and Services Regulatory Bureau (HFSRB) after applicants pass the committee’s exam. These are valid for three years and can be revoked if not renewed within five.
Students spend about two months in class and a month embalming real cadavers at partner funeral homes. Tuition ranges from about P27,000 to about P30,000 depending on the training institution.
Over half of Cribello’s students at PCAS have worked in funeral homes or come from families that own one. His oldest student was 75; the average age is around 45.
“It’s such a unique challenge because people [are] going back to school after years of not having a good habit of reading or studying,” he said.

PCAS now runs two cohorts a year of about 60 students each, up from 10 per cohort in 2009. At PEURTC in Manila, where Ovejera still teaches, local classes run 40 to 60 students, plus a separate class of five to eight from neighboring Southeast Asian countries like Singapore, Thailand, and Malaysia who come to the Philippines for mortuary education. Affordability and English as a medium of instruction are the main attractions.

blocks.caption: EMBALMING. Tools and chemicals found in an embalming preparation room at Arlington Memorial Chapels in Quezon City, Manila. Jake Gomez/Rappler

blocks.text: Philippine embalmers train on only a handful of tools and chemicals. In the US, Cribello estimated, training incorporates 30 to 35 pieces of equipment.
“There are very simple kinds and sets of tools that have been used in the past and continue to be taught today here. That much has not changed,” he said.
Most local funeral homes rely on formalin, a cheap formaldehyde solution. Other chemicals used abroad, in what is called soft embalming, can make a face look more natural.
But culture and climate shape the practice, Ovejera said. Filipino wakes routinely run around the clock for days, sometimes weeks, and softer chemicals do not hold up in humid weather.

Cost matters too. A 200-liter drum of formalin costs around P11,000 to P15,000, while soft-embalming chemicals can cost 20 times more, according to Ovejera. For that reason, only select funeral homes offer more technical and upscale embalming options.
Demand for an embalmer’s work is guaranteed. Fair pay, Cribello said, is not.

“There is a certain opportunity to review the industry regulations in terms of the kind of salaries imposed within the industry,” Cribello said. “I personally feel that we are behind [compared with] similar professionals like nurses and doctors.”

Entry-level salaries still hover around minimum wage (P401 to P755 per day, depending on the region), according to PCAS and PEAP, and embalmers get no hazard pay despite chronic exposure to chemicals like formaldehyde, which the International Agency for Research on Cancer classifies as a Group 1 carcinogen.
The 2010 rules set minimum wage as the entry point, Ovejera said, but smaller funeral homes often pay per body instead, pushing many embalmers to freelance and work between funerary businesses.
Change in any regard would require legislation. “I agree that there must be changes. But how do we do that? It has to be in legislation,” Ovejera said.

Embalmers also have no seat on the body that licenses them. Under the current rules, the DOH-CEUE’s five members are a chairperson, vice chairperson, sanitary engineer, pathologist, and legal officer. No mention of an embalmer sitting on the committee of examiners.
Licensed embalmers take part only as assessors for the oral and practical exam. By contrast, the board that licenses nurses is made up of nurses.
The number of active, licensed embalmers in the country is hard to pin down.

The DOH-CEUE has not formally published updated figures in recent years, according to PCAS. The embalmers association recorded about 5,000 licensed embalmers in 2018, though that count includes those who have died, moved abroad, or let their licenses lapse.

Exams were suspended in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic. Since resumption, each exam has licensed roughly 100 people, bringing the total to between 6,000 and 6,300, according to the embalmers association. PCAS estimates 200 to 300 new embalmers a year.
In March 2026, 75 aspirants earned their licenses. After the September 2026 written exam, 125 moved on to the oral and practical portion.
Better data would help as Singapore, Malaysia, and employers in the Middle East, Europe, and North America look to hire Filipino embalmers, Ovejera said.
“Without knowing the actual figures…we don’t even know: do we have enough [at home]?” Ovejera said.

The counts also miss a group that’s harder to track: people who embalm without a license, which DOH rules prohibit. Several embalmers we spoke with said the practice persists, particularly in provinces where training is inaccessible.
Both men remain hopeful that the industry will continue to catch up.

For Cribello, the work remains “the ultimate noble cause.” In his classes, he pushes the fundamentals of hygiene and care for grieving families, along with sounder business practices for a new generation of operators.
“While it’s [grim] and tiring, it gives fulfillment that I can have a platform where I can influence not just one student, but operators and embalmers all throughout the country,” he said.
For Ovejera, it became all the more personal in 2023, when his father died. “I wanted to make sure that we do the best for him,” he said. He helped embalm his father himself.

That experience, he said, further strengthened the importance of the work to grieving families. “The picture of an individual lying there inside the casket…will always be in the cognitive footprint of the family members,” he said.
PEAP has also explored ladderized programs through the introduction of embalming into more Filipino universities, Ovejera said. For now, it remains a short certificate course rather than a degree.
“There’s a lot more work to do… We want to be more globally competitive,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden hit by suspected cyber-attack
articles.summary: One store in Sweden says temperatures for its freezers were set to 50 C (122F).

blocks.text: Dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting its refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets and 15 Carrefour stores were affected in Belgium, while several ICA and Coop shops in Sweden were hit. Thirteen SuperValu shops have also been impacted in Ireland.
Thousands of euros worth of food has had to be thrown away, according to local media reports, with one ICA store in Sweden saying temperatures for its freezers had been set to 50 C (122F).
It is not clear who is behind the attack, which follows a similar incident last month that affected hundreds of French supermarkets.
Delhaize, one of Belgium's biggest supermarket chains, told Belgian media a "computer incident" had occurred overnight at 40 shops.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said it was "currently analysing" the incident at 15 of its Belgian stores.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for ICA in Sweden confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the IVA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden are also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

articles.title: Will renewed conflict derail Ethiopia's economic growth?
articles.summary: Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. But renewed fighting in the north of the BRICS member state could deter investment, strain public finances and push up the cost of living.

image.caption: Service and financial sector growth has transformed Addis Ababa's skyline. Could the new conflict halt the boom?Image: Solomon Muche/DW

blocks.text: Ethiopia's economy is growing strongly. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) forecasts real growth of 9.2% for the 2025–26 fiscal year. But renewed fighting in the north, high reconstruction costs and climate-related crop problems are threatening the country's economic recovery.

London-based financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the consequences of a renewed escalation. "If there is a major conflict [...] the current economic growth will not be sustainable," he told DW.

blocks.caption: Ethiopia's PM Abiy Ahmed visits an industrial park in Hawassa, the capital of the Sidama region, in August 2025Image: Ethiopian Prime Minister Office

blocks.text: The costly legacy of the Tigray war

The war that raged in Tigray and other parts of Ethiopia between 2020 and 2022 left extensive damage. Infrastructure was destroyed, businesses lost production capacity and agricultural land could no longer be cultivated in some areas.

A World Bank-backed damage and needs assessment puts the damage caused by several conflicts in Ethiopia between November 2020 and December 2021 at more than $22.6 billion (€20.2 billion). Economic losses amounted to around $6 billion. The estimated funding required for reconstruction and economic recovery stands at approximately $19.7 billion. This figure represents the total funding requirement, not annual costs or damage caused by the current escalation.
A reconstruction plan covered the period from 2023 to 2028. However, it remains uncertain whether the work can be fully funded and completed within that timeframe.

Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed believes the economic consequences of the Tigray war were even more severe. In addition to the direct destruction, he points to lost economic output, high inflation and foreign currency shortages at the time. International trade conditions also deteriorated: in 2022, Ethiopia lost its benefits under the US African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), which had allowed certain African exports to enter the US market duty-free.
Growth despite the crisis

Following the Pretoria peace agreement in November 2022, the economy began to recover. According to the IMF, it grew by 7.2% in 2022–23 and 8.1% in 2023–24. The organization puts growth at 9.2% for 2024–25 and forecasts a further 9.2% for 2025–26. Agriculture, mining and electricity generation are among the main drivers of this growth.

This does not contradict the economic damage caused by the war. Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the total economic output of a country. If major sectors outside conflict-affected areas continue to expand, the overall economy can grow even while individual regions are still suffering the consequences of violence.

However, high growth rates do not mean that the country's economic problems have been resolved. Reconstruction remains a major challenge, inflation continues to put pressure on households and the government has to service its debt. In late 2023, Ethiopia defaulted after missing an interest payment on a Eurobond. Reforms supported by an IMF program launched in 2024 are intended to address structural weaknesses in the economy.
Higher military spending, less money for development

A renewed escalation could put additional pressure on public finances. The government would have to spend more on military personnel, equipment and logistics. At the same time, economic activity and, consequently, tax revenues could decline in the affected regions.

"A substantial share of government resources would be tied up in military spending that would otherwise be available for infrastructure, education and social services," warned Abdulmenan Mohammed. The extent of this impact would depend on the scale and duration of any renewed conflict.

blocks.caption: Financial analyst Abdulmenan Mohammed warns of the economic consequences of a renewed escalationImage: privat

blocks.text: A prolonged war could also prompt businesses to postpone investments. International lenders and donors might become more cautious, while the government would need additional funds for security and humanitarian assistance. This could leave less money available for roads, energy infrastructure and other development projects.
Inflation and foreign currency shortages
The IMF forecasts an average inflation rate of 11.7% for 2025–26. Prices are therefore expected to continue rising, although at a slower pace than in previous years.

Abdulmenan Mohammed expects a further escalation to intensify inflationary pressures. "If the conflict escalates further, inflation is likely to rise," he said. To finance additional spending, the government might resort to more domestic borrowing. This could crowd out private businesses by making it harder for them to access credit and finance investments.

The military also needs foreign currency to purchase equipment from abroad. If this demand increases, fewer foreign exchange reserves could be available to private businesses for imports. This would put further pressure on the birr exchange rate and drive up the cost of imported goods, fuel and industrial inputs.

The extent of these effects on the BRICS member state would also depend on export earnings, monetary policy and developments in international markets. A new surge in inflation is therefore a risk, but not an inevitable consequence of the escalation. A combination of rising prices and uncertain incomes would be particularly difficult for poorer households.

blocks.caption: Around 750,000 people in Ethiopia remain internally displaced as a result of the Tigray conflictImage: Privat

blocks.text: Agriculture and tourism particularly vulnerable

Abdulmenan Mohammed sees agriculture, as well as the tourism and hospitality sectors, as particularly vulnerable. "Agriculture is especially exposed because much of the fighting takes place in rural areas where farmers work," he said.

Insecurity around farmland, disrupted transport routes and shortages of agricultural inputs can undermine production. At the same time, parts of the country are experiencing insufficient rainfall and poor harvest prospects. Failed harvests reduce farmers' incomes, while lower food supplies can push prices even higher.
Tourism is also highly sensitive to security risks. Travel advisories and reports of fighting can deter visitors, reducing revenues for hotels and tour operators.
Could neighboring countries benefit from the crisis?

When making investment decisions, international investors consider not only market size but also political stability, security and the reliability of state institutions. A further escalation could therefore delay investment decisions or prompt companies to consider alternative locations.

However, there is currently no concrete evidence that companies are already withdrawing investments from Ethiopia because of the fighting and relocating them to neighboring countries such as Kenya. Abdulmenan Mohammed also sees no demonstrable economic advantage for Kenya at this stage. Beyond security, factors such as tax administration, public services and governance also play a decisive role.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Democrats condemn Haley Stevens’ ‘betrayal’ following endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers – US politics live
articles.summary:
The latest move has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests

Some of the people who worked for Stevens’s campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers…

blocks.text: Democrats condemn Haley Stevens' 'betrayal' following Republican endorsement
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Democratic politicians have condemned congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, over her endorsement of his Republican rival just days before the midterm vote.

Stevens’ extraordinary endorsement of Mike Rogers was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
As one might expect, top Democrats have been quick to express their outrage at the congresswoman’s “betrayal”.

California governor Gavin Newsom said on the political talkshow 2WAY that Stevens “went another 180 degrees overnight, so something was going on there”. “She’s been successful at taking our eye off the ball and that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it ... This may be curiously the October surprise of sorts,” he added.

Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats. He said:

double quotation markSenate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans. These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.
Meanwhile, Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said:

double quotation markHaley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.

Bernie Sanders joined the controversy, attacking Stevens for what Democrats view as an extraordinary betrayal after Stevens accepted El-Sayed’s narrow victory over her in Michigan’s Democrat senate primaries.

“Rep. Haley Stevens’ staff is right to resign in disgust,” Sanders posted on X. “They understand that the election in Michigan is far more important than Haley’s fragile ego and that all of us must stand together to elect Abdul, defeat Rogers and end the Republican rubber-stamp control of the Senate.”
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said Stevens had “betrayed” working class people “by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against”.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:

items: Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”. The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. “If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump said.

A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses. Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.

Murphy, 53, started feeling numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday, according to the Connecticut senator’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. A hospital visit confirmed that Murphy had experienced a stroke.

articles.title: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.summary:
Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg said fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack that hit French stores in October

Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have…

blocks.text: Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.

Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.

The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.

Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.

“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”

French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.

Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.

Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.

Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.
after newsletter promotion

They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.

The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

articles.title: Russia bombs aid centre and shelter in southern Ukraine killing at least 24, officials say
articles.summary: Russia bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 24 people, Ukraine's emergency services agency said.

image.caption: Smoke rises over an underground shelter at a compound of a school after a Russian airstrike in the frontline town of Komyshuvakha, Ukraine. The school was used as a humanitarian aid hub. (National Police of Ukraine/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated
Russia bombed an aid distribution centre and neighbouring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 24 people, Ukraine's emergency services agency said.
Attack came a day after Ukraine, Russian emergency alert systems were hit by cyberattacks
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that 10 guided bombs targeted an area that included a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid and a nearby shelter.
"This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation," Zelenskyy said.

The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country's south. The limited ceasefire agreement had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas in Russian-occupied territory.

"There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible," Zelenskyy said. "With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings."

As night fell in Komyshuvakha, emergency responders used flashlights to search through the rubble of collapsed buildings, according to photos and video posted online by local officials. About 20 people are considered missing and the death toll could rise, these officials say.

Efforts to rescue people Monday evening were hindered as Russian drones launched additional attacks in the area that had been bombed, according to Mykhailo Semikin, a military official in Zaporizhzhia.

A screenshot of a phone shows a series of false alerts received late Sunday from an emergency alert app that was subject to a cyberattack, in Kyiv. The third message in Russian reads 'Hi! There will be a nuclear threat across Ukraine. Do not worry, the Oreshnik is incoming.' The fifth and sixth messages in Ukrainian read 'Increased danger, Go to the shelter.' (The Associated Press)
Attacks followed cyberattacks

Earlier, officials in Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert mobile apps were targeted by cyberattacks on Sunday, with users in Ukraine receiving false warnings of dangerously high radiation levels in the capital, Kyiv.

In a Telegram post late Sunday, Ukraine's air raid alert channel said "unauthorized parties" had interfered with the app's operation and that the service had been temporarily suspended. It warned users not to click on links in "suspicious notifications."

Authorities in Ukraine said the app, which Ukrainians rely on to seek safety amid daily Russian missile and drone strikes, was restored overnight. The alerts — making false claims of high radiation levels, a chemical threat and public disturbances in Kyiv — were written in English with spelling and grammatical errors, as well as in a mix of Russian and Ukrainian.
One of the false posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore.
Municipal employees in Odesa work at the site of homes that were damaged during a Russian drone strike on Monday, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine. (Nina Liashonok/Reuters)

Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. That claim could not be independently verified.

Ukraine's state-run Center for Countering Disinformation reported the breach and urged users to monitor emergency channels on social media and rely on physical alerts while the cyberattack was being addressed.
Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for Ukraine's air force command, said the cyberattack had no impact on Ukraine's security and defence operations because the app is separate from military command systems.
Ihnat told Ukraine's private 1+1 television channel that the air force continues to report real-time threats through independent communication channels, including popular social media platforms.

items: Trump's increasing support for Russia carries existential danger for Canada
Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky arrive in Ukraine-held territory

blocks.text: In Russia, officials said Monday that hackers had sent fake emergency alerts after gaining access to the Russian Emergency Ministry's mobile app.

The ministry did not name who carried out the attack. In a statement, it reassured Russians that the wider public alert system was working normally, and that the mobile app acted as a supplementary service alongside alerts shared through SMS messages, media broadcasts and municipal sirens and loudspeakers.
Limited ceasefire ends
In other fighting, Ukrainian authorities in the Kherson region reported multiple Russian drone attacks early Monday, hours after a humanitarian ceasefire expired.
The regional administration said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were hospitalized with blast injuries in the city of Kherson, across the Dnipro River from Russian-occupied territory.
This is how residents of the besieged town of Oleshky stayed alive
The localized ceasefire ended at midnight at the start of Monday. The brief pause in fighting was tied to a humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
The ceasefire, which began Oct. 27, marked the most significant truce between Kyiv and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began nearly five years ago.
The pause allowed besieged residents of Oleshky to be evacuated in a rare joint operation that ended Saturday.

An estimated 2,000 civilians were in Oleshky when the temporary truce took effect. They could evacuate to territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the city with replenished food and medical supplies. Exact evacuation totals were withheld to protect those who stayed.
Ukraine's general staff said Monday that Russia's military had bolstered its drone defences and replenished ammunition supplies in the area during the ceasefire.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, emergency services reported that drone strikes injured 12 people in the eastern Kharkiv region and damaged a refrigeration facility, greenhouses and residential buildings.
Five people were also reported injured in the Black Sea port city of Odesa, where a warehouse was targeted and homes were damaged.

articles.title: Five arrested after South African farmer shot and tortured
articles.summary: The attack on Donovan Marx, 50, comes as right-wing groups say there is a genocide of white people - a claim widely discredited.

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains graphic details that some people may find distressing
South African police have arrested five people in connection with a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.
Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.
Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.
All five of his alleged attackers were arrested over the weekend, a move welcomed by Marx's wife and family.
They added that the "legal process must [now] take its course".
The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.
Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.
A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.
The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.
When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.
"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."
The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.
The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.
Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.
South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".
The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.
The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, will appear in local courts on Tuesday and face house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition charges.

Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.

Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.
South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.
However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

blocks.text: The conference comes weeks before the opening of Duterte's trial scheduled on November 30
MANILA, Philippines – The International Criminal Court (ICC) will hold its fifth status conference on former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes against humanity case on Monday, November 2.
This comes weeks before the opening of the trial scheduled on November 30.
A status conference is where parties discuss matters related to the case before proceeding to a full trial.

So far, the court has had four conferences: on May 27, when it announced that the trial will begin on November 30; on June 23, when the chamber cautioned lawyers against granting media interviews; and the third one, on September 16, when the former president made an appearance.
The court held the fourth conference on October 13, where the parties discussed the list of evidence anew.
Duterte will skip the Monday hearing after waiving his right to be present.
For the fifth status conference, the Trial Chamber III and the parties will discuss the following:

Audio-visual link testimony and rights of audience
List of witnesses and number of hours for the Prosecution’s presentation of evidence

articles.summary: The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request…

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published November 2, 2026 6:43pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III that will hear the crimes against humanity charges against former President Rodrigo Duterte has rejected the counsel for the victims' request that portions of their opening statement be delivered in Tagalog.

This was one of the measures that the trial chamber decided in its fifth pre-trial conference at the ICC in The Hague. Duterte was not present at the conference on Monday after the court granted the defense's request that he not attend.

Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said allowing Tagalog—which is not among the ICC’s official languages—would complicate victim applications and significantly increase trial costs because of translation requirements.
The request was raised by Public Counsel for Victims Paolina Massidda, who argued that using Tagalog was necessary to accurately convey the victims' narratives.
Massida noted that the use of Tagalog would be strictly limited to quoting victims and would not be used throughout the entire opening statement.
Under the Rome Statute, the official languages of the ICC are English and French. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: [New Rx] What if the Philippines leased an island for 100 years?
articles.summary: Hong Kong can be a model. Singapore and South Korea might bring in long-term capital, drive regional economic growth, and spark broader national governance reforms in the Philippines

blocks.text: The Philippine peso recently reached a record low of ₱64.17 against the US dollar. While currency depreciation alone does not indicate economic weakness, it raises a key question: how can the Philippines strengthen investor confidence and attract long-term capital for economic transformation?
During a visit to the Philippines, my father made an unusual suggestion: why not lease one island to another country for 100 years?

Under this proposal, the partner country would help establish a distinct legal and institutional framework while the Philippines retains sovereignty, national defense, and responsibility for essential public services. After a century, the Philippines would inherit a thriving economic center with modern infrastructure and competitive institutions.

In January 2016, then-presidential candidate Rodrigo Duterte proposed leasing islands to multinational companies with autonomy to develop infrastructure and operating rules. However, my father’s proposal differs: rather than relying on private corporations, it involves a government-to-government institutional partnership.

The historical comparison is Hong Kong. In 1898, China leased the New Territories to Britain for 99 years. Decades later, Hong Kong helped channel international capital, expertise, and commerce into Shenzhen and the Pearl River Delta, illustrating how a jurisdiction with distinct institutions can stimulate development far beyond its borders.

The Philippines already offers investment incentives and special economic zones, but these remain subject to the national administrative framework. What if one island operated under a distinct system of civil and commercial laws, an independent judiciary, taxation, and regulatory institutions?

The goal would be to offer investors predictable rules, enforceable contracts, and credible institutions. Like Hong Kong, it could feature separate residency arrangements while preserving Philippine citizenship.

Importantly, the foreign partner would not operate the entire government. The Philippines would continue providing healthcare, education, policing, municipal services, and defense. The partner would supply the institutional architecture: judicial expertise, regulatory standards, and independent oversight.

Such an arrangement would require constitutional changes, particularly to establish an independent judiciary and a distinct immigration system. The experiment would concern institutions, not merely financial incentives.

Singapore’s domestic market is small, land and labor are constrained, and its companies need international expansion. Initiatives like the Johor-Singapore Special Economic Zone demonstrate its strategy of pairing financial and technological strengths with regional land and workforce capacity.

A Philippine island could offer another variation of that strategy. Singaporean businesses could establish manufacturing facilities, logistics hubs, and research campuses operating under familiar standards. Headquarters and advanced research would remain in Singapore, while land-intensive operations locate on the island.
Unlike conventional industrial parks, the arrangement would feature a separate judicial and regulatory framework supported by Singaporean institutions.

Private investors could finance much of the infrastructure, limiting Singaporean taxpayer exposure while Singapore contributes institutional expertise rather than assuming territorial administration. Singapore has not expressed interest in such an arrangement, and its potential participation would require further examination.

Alternatively, South Korea brings strengths in advanced manufacturing, engineering, and digital governance. The partner could be any country with strong institutions, proven administrative capabilities, and no territorial ambitions.

Imagine an underdeveloped island transformed into an international commercial center with modern ports, industrial parks, and universities. The benefits would extend to surrounding provinces supplying agriculture, labor, and materials, stimulating investment across the region. Any location would require an independent feasibility study and a credible process for securing the informed consent of affected communities.

To protect Philippine sovereignty, foreign military bases and territorial claims would be prohibited. The Philippines would retain national defense and natural resource rights, while existing residents’ citizenship, property rights, and political representation would be protected. Equally important, foreign partners would need assurances against unilateral termination by future Philippine administrations. A constitutionally authorized bilateral treaty, international arbitration, compensation provisions, and political-risk insurance could reduce these risks, although no legal safeguard could entirely eliminate them.

Beyond economics, experiencing predictable permits, efficient dispute resolution, and transparent rules could raise public expectations for governance across the Philippines, encouraging broader national reforms. The island’s greatest legacy might be changing what Filipinos expect from the government.

The Philippines has pursued growth through incentives and economic zones for decades. The next experiment should focus on institutional credibility. By starting with just one island, the Philippines could create a model that delivers capital, infrastructure, and institutional learning for generations to come. After 100 years, the Philippines could inherit not only a thriving economic center but also institutions and practices worth adopting elsewhere.

Speaking in Parliament in 1977 about Singapore’s need to develop its own institutional approach, then-Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew expressed a philosophy that remains relevant far beyond its original context:
“We have got to find our own style. We have got to be bold enough to experiment.” – Rappler.com

Dr. Jaemin Park is an adjunct professor at the University of the Philippines College of Public Health and works across Southeast Asia on healthcare financing, medical innovation, and public sector reform.

articles.title: [Rappler’s Best] America, your turn
articles.summary: The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as President Donald Trump enters the last two years of his term

blocks.text: The past week thrilled liberals and leftists across the world as elections in three polarized countries stemmed the march of the far-right in Latin America, demonstrated student power in Europe, and humbled Benjamin Netanyahu.
These polls have been hard fought, but the post-election transitions will be doubly harder.

items: Crying fraud but also facing corruption charges back home, Flavio Bolsonaro, Brazil’s defeated presidential candidate, has fled to the US into the welcoming arms of his patron, US President Donald Trump. Bolsonaro can stay in America for as long as he wants, Trump said. His father, Jair, a former president, is in jail in Brazil.

Running on an anti-corruption wave, Serbia’s student protest movement managed to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic in an election, but now comes the hard part of governing. For starters, the student leaders have called for the resignation of top public officials and investigations into alleged corruption under Vucic.

In Israel, the far-right continues to dominate, but did not come out solidly for Netanyahu, whose party lost the majority in parliament. Without any bloc enjoying majority numbers, however, he will likely serve as caretaker prime minister. How could Israel break an election deadlock? Here’s an explainer.

blocks.text: And so we turn to the next logical question: what will America show the rest of the world this week?
The US midterm elections are happening on November 3, and the results will determine control of Congress as Trump enters the last two years of his term. Here are things to know.

If you’re a liberal and listened to pollster Nate Silver’s interview with Ezra Klein (as I did), you’d be expecting a “momentous” turnaround — a more than 70% chance for Democrats in the Senate — that could flip Congress against Trump. If the results reflect what he’s seeing in his polling, Silver said these would effectively end the Trump era.

The Economist has more conservative numbers. While conceding that the “auguries are good for Democrats,” it’s putting the probability of the US Senate going to the Democrats at just 54%. But the White House is already crafting a path to govern without Congress in case Democrats win, according to a Reuters report.

items: These are the races that will decide control of the US Senate, and the key seats that could shape the next House.

The campaign period has been reminiscent of traditional tactics in Philippine elections, writes Filipino-American Oscar Quiambao in this piece. There have been concerns about Republican efforts to delay the vote counts and intimidate voters. And let’s not forget that Trump himself offered $5,000 to every American if Republicans win.
There are four ways foreign policy could change if Democrats win this week.

blocks.text: This also marks the first elections in the US where voters have been relying on chatbots to guide them. It’s a cautionary tale.

items: A study showed almost 40% of chatbots’ replies to election-related queries contained at least one factual error. Read more.

The flood of AI-driven disinformation has been unprecedented, according to this story, which cites one instance when the Democrat running for US Senate in Texas (a Republican base), James Talarico, had to take time off from campaigning due to flu. A fake video about him supposedly being treated at a mental health facility in Ohio went viral.
Russia is apparently fueling fake reports about Democrats, according to an intelligence briefing that US lawmakers received. Read more.
Outside the US, in Brazil, AI content bypassed election rules — a lesson for the Philippines, writes Alex Culla in this story.

blocks.text: As Trump spent the past days doing his final push for a Republican win, his defense chief Pete Hegseth flew to Cebu for the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting. There, the host, Philippine Defense Secretary Gibo Teodoro, snubbed the Chinese defense attaché who ranked lower than him. Bea Cupin gives us a recap of the meeting in this report.
On another note, we extend our deepest condolences to the family of Philip Juico, who died on October 31 after years of battling cancer.

articles.title: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.summary: Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson says the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran

blocks.text: Iranian negotiators have left talks with Qatari mediators aimed at ending the war with the United States, and a draft proposal is being circulated with a follow-up meeting possible, an official briefed on the talks said on Monday, November 2.
The negotiators departed on Sunday, November 1, though not because of difficulties in the negotiations, the official said, without providing further details on the draft proposal.

Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said the basis of the talks is a seven-step plan Iran drew up in September to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the US naval blockade on Iran, with Tehran now suggesting that proposal could be implemented on a faster timeline under a deal.
The spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi had been in Doha to facilitate the exchange of messages with Washington via Qatari intermediaries.

“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently. These demands are reasonable and logical: No final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought to an end, Iran’s demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” Baghaei said.

On Saturday, Qatari broadcaster Al Jazeera quoted Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi as saying that under a deal the Strait of Hormuz could be opened within a two-day timeline rather than within the seven days originally envisaged.
Iran’s initial proposal was rejected by US President Donald Trump.

The latest round of diplomacy comes amid concerns that the conflict could escalate again after Tuesday’s midterm elections in the United States. Asked about Tehran’s view on the midterms, Baghaei said Tehran did not expect elections to “give birth to a new US.”
Trump has said the United States would not launch new attacks on Iran before the vote and that talks with Tehran have been productive, though he has not ruled out further military action.

articles.title: Senate majority united in stripping 2027 budget bill of ‘corruption-prone items’ – Lacson
articles.summary: Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget

blocks.text: PING LACSON. Senator Ping Lacson speaks during the Senate plenary debates on the 2026 budget on November 18, 2025.
Senate PRIB
Senator Ping Lacson says no one will be spared in their bid to 'cleanse' the proposed 2027 budget
MANILA, Philippines – The Senate majority bloc is united in removing “corruption-prone” items from the House-approved version of the proposed 2027 national budget, Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson said.

“The majority of senators are rallying behind Senate finance committee chairman JV Ejercito’s efforts to cleanse the 2027 budget of unwarranted, whimsical, and corruption-prone items — all means all!” Lacson said in a social media post.

Over the weekend, Lacson said Ejercito had secured the commitment of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) that it will submit all supporting documents for its infrastructure projects by Tuesday, November 3. Projects without the required documents would be removed from the House-approved version of the 2027 General Appropriations Bill (GAB).
Budget advocacy groups, including the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC) and BetterGovPH, had flagged nearly 7,000 projects worth P190 billion with no published project attachments in the HGAB.

A separate Senate review also found that the number of DPWH projects had increased from 11,420 in the National Expenditure Program (NEP) to 16,244 in the House-approved GAB. Of these, 6,271 were new projects introduced by lawmakers without prior vetting by the executive branch.
Lacson also said Ejercito would invite civil society organizations to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the budget, which would be livestreamed to promote transparency.
The Senate will take up the budget bill when plenary sessions resume on November 9, with plenary debates expected to begin on November 23. – Rappler.com

articles.title: BI nabs alleged JP Dragon crime syndicate leader in Cabanatuan
articles.summary: A Japanese fugitive, reportedly among the leaders of the transnational criminal syndicate JP Dragon, was arrested during an operation in Cabanatuan City on October 31, the Bureau of Immigration (BI)…

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 5:36pm

A Japanese fugitive, reportedly among the leaders of the transnational criminal syndicate JP Dragon, was arrested during an operation in Cabanatuan City on October 31, the Bureau of Immigration (BI) said Sunday.

The bureau identified the Japanese citizen as 57-year-old Yamamoto Yoshitama, who is wanted in Japan for fraud, theft, and attempted theft under an arrest warrant issued by the Fukuoka Summary Court on December 27, 2022.

According to BI Fugitive Search Unit Chief Rendel Ryan Sy, Yamamoto was allegedly among the leaders of JP Dragon, a Japan-based criminal syndicate "composed largely of former yakuza members and believed to operate primarily in Metro Manila."

“The group has been linked to sophisticated telephone fraud schemes targeting elderly Japanese citizens. Its members allegedly impersonate police officers to deceive victims into surrendering their ATM cards and banking information,” BI said.
“Japanese investigators suspect that the syndicate defrauded approximately 250 victims of around ¥900 million (around Php362 million) since 2019,” it added.
Yamamoto is expected to be held at the BI Warden’s Facility while awaiting deportation proceedings.

Immigration Commissioner Joel Anthony Viado said the Philippines will not be a "safe haven" for foreign fugitives, adding that the bureau will ensure the country's borders remain secure against international criminals seeking refuge.

The BI said it remains committed to sustaining its operations against foreign fugitives and maintaining close coordination with local and international law enforcement agencies. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/RF, GMA News

articles.title: What does the Million Mask March mean for the Philippines?
articles.summary: Hacktivist activity related to the Million Mask March of a given year tends to fluctuate depending on issues brought up or simmering in the interim

blocks.text: Guy Fawkes mask image from Fauve/Wikimedia Commons
Hacktivist activity related to the Million Mask March of a given year tends to fluctuate depending on issues brought up or simmering in the interim

items: The Million Mask March, a global protest event held on November 5, originated from the hacking collective Anonymous and is associated with themes of political dissent and activism.

Past events, particularly in 2013, saw significant online defacements of Philippine government websites as a precursor to the protests, highlighting issues like political corruption and police violence.

The upcoming 2026 Million Mask March may be influenced by recent controversies within the Philippine Department of Information and Communications Technology, potentially leading to renewed protest actions.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – If you see a defaced Philippine government website this early in November, it could be a one-off event, but it also may be a single defacement of many, owing to a movement called the Million Mask March.

The Million Mask March is a worldwide day of protest held on November 5 and is also colloquially known as “Operation Vendetta,” after the movie and British graphic novel V for Vendetta, wherein the main character of the story wears a Guy Fawkes mask.

Originally set up by hacking collective Anonymous, the Million Mask March began in 2012 with the largest events occurring outside the Philippines, such as in London in the United Kingdom and Washington DC in the United States.

The event is usually preceded by hacking activities or online defacements of websites to drum up interest and sentiment in conducting a Million Mask March in a given locality. These defacements and hacks decry a number of issues, such as political corruption, police violence and militarization.
This was most strongly felt in the early iterations of the protest, especially in the Philippines’ 2013 Million Mask March, which saw more than 30 Philippine government websites crashed or defaced.

A video from Anonymous on the affected sites back then apologized for the disruption but called on citizens to join the November 5 protest action. In response, police at the time also took steps to maintain public safety, but also invited protesters in for questioning.
Activity related to Million Mask March tends to fluctuate depending on the time frame of issues brought up.

While the 2025 Million Mask March was apparently less pronounced and did not receive as much media coverage save for notices in online hacking communities, there’s no telling what might spur on a 2026 protest action.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) could possibly be in for a long few days of work though, seeing as there is a new DICT secretary, former Social Security System chief Robert Joseph de Claro,.

There also seeming loss of trust in the institution owing to the actions — and resignation — of the previous DICT secretary, Henry Aguda, as regards the temporary banning of Discord and the threat to ban other services that may be responsible for the spread of nihilistic violent extremism.

There’s also the preventive suspension of DICT eGov Undersecretary David Almirol over alleged conflicts of interest in the eGov app and the system’s development, which may bring an opportunity for bad actors or hacker-activists to take advantage of the situation.

blocks.caption: Conflict of interest? Audit questions DICT usec’s ties to former company Multisys

blocks.text: Unfortunately, there’s no telling what could spark strong protest actions on November 5 in the Philippines, and it’s just as difficult to determine if an informal Million Mask March is coming this year.
Perhaps it’s better to remember the fifth of November as a day when plans to bring injustices to the forefront of public consciousness comes to a head.
Though in this country, that may as well be any given weekday. – Rappler.com

Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant…

blocks.text: Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant minister starts to give the details in a statement to MPs, Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, erupts with fury and rants and raves at the Treasury bench about how all the main points have already been leaked to the media, in contravention of the ministerial code.

Not today. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will this afternoon unveil the final version of her plans to make foreign workers wait longer before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain, and we know relatively little about what she will say. The original plans were unveiled last November and they would require most workers to wait 10 years, not five, for ILR, with care workers having to wait 15 years. They would also apply to foreign workers already here, not just new arrivals. These proposals were hugely controversial, and Andy Burnham himself was among the ministers arguing that care workers should be treated more kindly.
As Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh report in our overnight story, there has been some sort of climbdown in relation to care workers.
But it also seems to be the case that the broad thrust of the plan is being retained and that ILR rules are being toughened in a way that will affect hundreds of thousands of people.

The detail, which is coming after 3.30pm, will be crucial; so will the reaction of Labour MPs. When Mahmood announced these plans last autumn, some government backbenchers were horrified. But mostly public condemnation was muted. At the time Reform UK had a lead of more than 10 points over Labour in the polls and Mahmood – who was arguing that net migration was too high and that low-skilled foreign workers ended up being a burden on the taxpayer (a key Reform UK claim, although one contested by experts) – was pushing at an open door.
Now the situation is very different. The electoral threat from Nigel Farage has receded quite a lot. And net migration is falling like a stone. Here are the figures from last week’s OBR report.

blocks.caption: Net migration figures Photograph: OBR

blocks.text: To implement the ILR changes, Mahmood does not need primary legislation and that means there will be no chance for potential Labour rebels to amend the plans in the Commons. But it has been reported that more than 100 MPs are queasy about what is being planned.

And Andy Burnham himself has accepted that the context has changed. We won’t hear from him until much later, because he is spending most of the day on a flight to the Commonwealth summit. But, in an interview for an ITV documentary being broadcast tomorrow, he declined to say that net migration was too high. When Keir Starmer was PM, he regularly did say this, and that he wanted immigration to fall “significantly”. Burnham told ITV small boat crossing numbers were “too high, for certain”. However, asked about legal migration, he replied:

double quotation markIt’s come right down. And I think when you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say is it too high or too low, because it’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy.
Burnham said legal migration had “come right down”. He declined to be drawn on whether it had to come down further.

This means that Mahmood will today be defending plans drawn up in response to a problem that some might argue no longer exists. However, speaking in the Commons last November, Mahmood argued she had to do something about the “so-called Boriswave, specifically the cohort of lower-qualified workers who – along with their dependants – entered the country through the health and care visa” because some of them were “never expected to be net economic contributors”, making “more stringent” controls needed.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
12.30pm: Danny Kruger, Reform UK’s head of government preparations, gives a speech to the Policy Exchange thinktank.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives her statement on the changes to indefinite leave to remain rules.
Evening: Andy Burnham arrives in Antigua for the Commonwealth summit.

Also, at some point today Labour will give an update on how many power-sharing agreements at council level with Greens will continue, in the light of Labour HQ saying recently Labour councillors should only continue to work with local Green parties willing to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green conference.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.
